questions.prompt: Which of the following organizations publishes guidelines for writing procedures and policies in the urinalysis?
questions.explanation: The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI; formerly NCCLS) publishes national and international consensus guidelines and standards for clinical laboratory testing, including GP16-A3 for urinalysis and guidelines for establishing procedure manuals. OSHA regulates occupational safety, the CDC monitors disease patterns and issues public health recommendations, and CLIA sets federal regulatory quality standards enforced by CMS. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book pp. 50, 62; PDF pp. 75, 87).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Exposure to toxic, carcinogenic, or caustic agents is what type of laboratory safety hazard?
questions.explanation: Exposure to toxic, carcinogenic, or caustic chemicals represents a chemical hazard. Biological hazards stem from infectious agents or biological specimens; sharps hazards originate from needles, lancets, and broken glass; and fire/explosive hazards involve open flames or flammable reagents. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book pp. 50, 56; PDF pp. 75, 81).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: In the urinalysis laboratory, the primary source in the chain of infection would be:
questions.explanation: The chain of infection requires an infectious agent, a reservoir, a portal of exit, a means of transmission, a portal of entry, and a susceptible host. In the urinalysis laboratory, patient urine and body fluid specimens serve as the primary reservoir and source of potential bloodborne pathogens and microorganisms. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book pp. 50–51; PDF pp. 75–76).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The best way to break the chain of infection is:
questions.explanation: Proper hand hygiene (hand washing or sanitizing) is recognized by the CDC and OSHA as the single most critical and effective procedure to prevent infection transmission and break the chain of infection in healthcare settings. Personal protective equipment, aerosol prevention, and surface decontamination are important complementary measures but do not substitute for routine hand hygiene. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book pp. 50, 54; PDF pp. 75, 79).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The current routine infection control policy developed by CDC and followed in all health-care settings is:
questions.explanation: Standard Precautions are the routine infection control policies established by the CDC and Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC). Standard Precautions combine Universal Precautions (blood and bloodborne pathogens) and Body Substance Isolation (all body fluids, secretions, and excretions except sweat) to protect healthcare workers and patients. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 51; PDF p. 76).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An employee who is accidentally exposed to a possible bloodborne pathogen should immediately:
questions.explanation: Following any accidental occupational exposure to blood or potential bloodborne pathogens, the incident must be reported immediately to a supervisor so that confidential medical evaluation, source individual documentation, and prompt postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) can begin within the critical post-exposure therapeutic window. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 53; PDF p. 78).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Personnel in the urinalysis laboratory should wear laboratory coats that:
questions.explanation: Protective laboratory coats worn in the urinalysis section must be fluid-resistant to prevent urine and body fluid splashes from soaking through to underlying personal clothing or nonintact skin. They should be completely closed (buttoned or snapped) and possess knit cuffs to keep sleeves out of hazardous biofluid containers. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 54; PDF p. 79).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following should be discarded in biohazardous waste containers except:
questions.explanation: Urine is generally not treated as biohazardous under standard waste disposal rules unless visibly contaminated with blood or specified by local regulations; therefore, empty urine specimen containers can typically be discarded in non-biohazardous solid waste. In contrast, blood collection tubes, decontamination towels, and contaminated disposable coats must always be placed into dedicated biohazardous waste receptacles. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 55; PDF p. 80).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An employer who fails to provide sufficient gloves for the employees may be fined by the:
questions.explanation: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) is the federal regulatory body authorized to establish and enforce workplace health and safety standards. OSHA has the legal authority to inspect clinical laboratories, issue citations, and assess financial penalties against employers who fail to supply adequate PPE (including properly fitted gloves). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 53; PDF p. 78).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An acceptable disinfectant for decontamination of blood and body fluids is:
questions.explanation: A 1:10 dilution of household bleach (sodium hypochlorite) prepared freshly every 24 hours is the standard, EPA-approved laboratory disinfectant for cleaning work surfaces contaminated with blood and infectious body fluids. Antimicrobial soaps are intended for skin, hydrogen peroxide is not standard for large laboratory surface decontamination, and sodium hydroxide is a caustic chemical, not a surface disinfectant. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 55; PDF p. 80).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Correct hand washing includes all of the following except:
choices: Rinsing hands in a downward position
Turning on the water with a paper towel
questions.officialAnswer: Turning on the water with a paper towel
questions.explanation: During hand washing, the worker wets hands under running warm water (turned on with bare hands before washing begins), applies soap, rubs vigorously to create friction and lather for at least 20 seconds, and rinses hands facing downward. Finally, a clean paper towel is used to dry hands and then to turn off the faucet handles to prevent recontaminating clean hands from contaminated faucet surfaces. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 54; PDF p. 79).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Centrifuging an uncapped specimen may produce a biological hazard in the form of:
questions.explanation: Centrifuging uncapped specimen containers produces airborne droplets and micro-aerosols of potentially infectious biofluids. Centrifuges must always be operated with securely capped tubes or sealed safety buckets/cups to prevent aerosol dispersion. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 55; PDF p. 80).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An employee who accidentally spills acid on his arm should immediately:
choices: Neutralize the acid with a base
Hold the arm under running water for 15 minutes
Wrap the arm in gauze and go to the emergency department
questions.officialAnswer: Hold the arm under running water for 15 minutes
questions.explanation: The immediate first-aid measure for skin contact with caustic acids or hazardous chemicals is to immediately flood the exposed area with copious amounts of running water using a safety shower or eyewash station for a minimum of 15 minutes. Attempting to apply neutralizing substances or ointments can trigger exothermic reactions and worsen tissue necrosis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 56; PDF p. 81).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: When combining acid and water, ensure that:
choices: Water is slowly added to acid
questions.explanation: When diluting concentrated acids, acid must always be slowly added to water ('Add Acid to Water', remembered as 'A&W'). Pouring water into concentrated acid causes localized rapid heat generation and explosive steam eruptions that can splatter concentrated acid onto the laboratory worker. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 57; PDF p. 82).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An employee can learn the carcinogenic potential of potassium chloride by consulting the:
questions.explanation: Under the OSHA Hazard Communication Standard and GHS guidelines, Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) must be readily accessible for every hazardous chemical in the workplace. Section 11 of the standardized SDS specifies toxicological data, health effects, and carcinogenic classifications. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book pp. 57–58; PDF pp. 82–83).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Employees should not work with radioisotopes if they are:
questions.explanation: Ionizing radiation carries substantial teratogenic and mutagenic risks to rapidly dividing fetal tissues; pregnant laboratory personnel should not work directly with open radioactive sources, and female workers should notify supervisors of potential or confirmed pregnancies to ensure dosimeter monitoring or reassignment. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 59; PDF p. 84).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are safe to do when removing the source of an electric shock except:
choices: Pulling the person away from the instrument
Using a glass container to move the instrument
questions.officialAnswer: Pulling the person away from the instrument
questions.explanation: When disconnecting electrical equipment, the plug housing itself must be grasped and pulled straight out of the wall outlet. Yanking on the electrical cord damages internal wire insulation, exposing live conductors and creating severe shock or electrical fire hazards. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 59; PDF p. 84).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The acronym PASS refers to:
questions.explanation: The acronym PASS standardizes the operational steps for deploying a portable fire extinguisher: Pull the pin, Aim the nozzle or hose at the base of the fire, Squeeze the operating levers together, and Sweep slowly from side to side across the burning fuel base. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 60; PDF p. 85).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The system used by firefighters to assess the risk potential when a fire occurs in the laboratory is:
questions.explanation: The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) Standard 704 diamond is the standardized warning system utilized by firefighters and emergency responders to rapidly identify the severity of health (blue), flammability (red), instability/reactivity (yellow), and specific (white) hazards in an emergency area. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 57; PDF p. 82).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A class ABC fire extinguisher contains:
questions.explanation: Class ABC multipurpose extinguishers contain dry chemical powders (typically monoammonium phosphate) capable of extinguishing ordinary combustibles (Class A), flammable liquids (Class B), and energized electrical equipment (Class C). Water extinguishers are strictly Class A; CO2 is effective for Classes B and C; Halon alternatives are used for delicate electronics. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 60; PDF p. 85).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The first thing to do when a fire is discovered is to:
questions.explanation: When a fire is discovered, the institutional response follows RACE: (R) Rescue anyone in immediate danger, (A) Activate the fire Alarm, (C) Contain the fire by closing doors, and (E) Extinguish the fire if small or Evacuate the area. Rescuing endangered personnel is the immediate first priority. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 60; PDF p. 85).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: If a red rash is observed after removing gloves, the employee:
choices: May be washing her hands too often
May have developed a latex allergy
Should not rub her hands so vigorously
questions.officialAnswer: May have developed a latex allergy
questions.explanation: A localized red rash, erythema, pruritus, or urticaria following glove removal indicates contact dermatitis or a developing Type I or Type IV allergic hypersensitivity to natural rubber latex proteins. The worker should report the symptoms to their supervisor and transition to non-latex (nitrile or neoprene) gloves. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 54; PDF p. 79).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Pipetting by mouth is:
choices: Acceptable for urine but not serum
Acceptable for reagents but not specimens
questions.explanation: Mouth pipetting is strictly prohibited in modern clinical laboratories for any substance, including urine, serum, nonhazardous reagents, and distilled water. Mechanical pipetting devices (bulb aspirators, pipet aids, or micropipettes) must be used exclusively to prevent ingestion and aspiration hazards. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 53; PDF p. 78).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The NPFA classification symbol contains information on all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The NFPA 704 symbol contains four color-coded quadrants: blue (health hazard), red (flammability), yellow (instability/reactivity), and white (special hazards like W with a slash or OX). Biohazards are denoted by the distinct international biohazard symbol on separate labels and are not categorized on the NFPA diamond. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 57; PDF p. 82).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The GHS requires the following on a chemical label:
choices: Biohazard symbol, warning sign, environmental impact
Hazard pictogram, signal words, hazard statement
Biological symbol, hazard pictogram, long-term effects
Signal words, hazard statement, biological symbol
questions.officialAnswer: Hazard pictogram, signal words, hazard statement
questions.explanation: The Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) requires secondary container labels to display a standardized hazard pictogram (black symbol on a white background with a red diamond border), a signal word ('Danger' or 'Warning'), hazard statements, and precautionary statements. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 58; PDF p. 83).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The classification of a fire that can be extinguished with water is:
questions.explanation: Class A fires involve ordinary solid combustible materials such as paper, cardboard, wood, and textiles. Water cools and quenches Class A fuels effectively. In contrast, water should never be applied to Class B (flammable liquid), Class C (electrical), or Class D (combustible metal) fires. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 60; PDF p. 85).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Employers are required to provide free immunization for:
questions.explanation: The OSHA Bloodborne Pathogen Standard mandates that healthcare employers offer the hepatitis B vaccination series free of charge to all employees whose duties involve potential exposure to blood or other potentially infectious body fluids. Vaccines for HIV and HCV do not exist, and other immunizations are not federally mandated for employer provision in the same standard. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 52; PDF p. 77).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A possible physical hazard in the hospital is:
questions.explanation: Physical hazards encompass environmental factors that can cause accidental bodily trauma, such as wet or slick floors, running in hallways, trailing power cords, open drawers, and improper lifting practices. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 61; PDF p. 86).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Quality management refers to:
choices: Quality of specimens and patient care
questions.officialAnswer: Quality of specimens and patient care
questions.explanation: Quality management (QM) refers to the overarching operational framework encompassing all preexamination (preanalytical), examination (analytical), and postexamination (postanalytical) processes to ensure accurate, timely, and clinically reliable laboratory test results. Quality control (QC) is the analytical component within QM. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book pp. 61–62; PDF pp. 86–87).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: During laboratory accreditation inspections, procedure manuals are examined for the presence of:
questions.explanation: Accreditation organizations (such as CAP, The Joint Commission, and CLIA inspectors) mandate that all laboratory standard operating procedure (SOP) manuals be reviewed, updated, and documented annually by the designated laboratory director or section supervisor. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 62; PDF p. 87).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: As the supervisor of the urinalysis laboratory, you have just adopted a new procedure. You should:
choices: Put the package insert in the procedure manual
Put a complete, referenced procedure in the manual
Put a cost analysis study in the procedure manual
questions.officialAnswer: Put a complete, referenced procedure in the manual
questions.explanation: Whenever an analytical procedure or reporting policy is revised, the new SOP must be formally reviewed, approved, dated, and signed by the laboratory director or designated supervisor before clinical implementation, and the staff must be trained and documented. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 62; PDF p. 87).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt:
Indicate whether each of the following would be considered a 1) preexamination, 2) examination, or 3) postexamination factor by placing the appropriate number in the blank:

1. Reagent expiration date
2. Rejecting a contaminated specimen
3. Constructing a Levy-Jennings chart
4. Telephoning a positive Clinitest result on a newborn
5. Calibrating the centrifuge
6. Collecting a timed urine specimen
questions.explanation: In clinical quality management: (1) Preexamination factors occur before analysis (rejecting contaminated specimens, collecting timed specimens); (2) Examination factors occur during analysis (monitoring reagent expiration dates, plotting Levey-Jennings control charts, calibrating centrifuges); (3) Postexamination factors occur after analysis (telephoning critical positive Clinitest results on a newborn). The official mapping sequence is 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book pp. 62–68; PDF pp. 87–93).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The testing of a specimen from an outside agency and the comparison of results with participating laboratories is called:
questions.explanation: Proficiency testing (PT) is an external quality assessment mechanism in which an approved external agency (e.g., CAP) distributes blind, unknown specimens to laboratories for analysis; the laboratory's reported results are scored against national consensus target values to evaluate analytical competency. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 67; PDF p. 92).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A color change indicating that a sufficient amount of a patient’s specimen or reagent is added correctly to the test system would be an example of:
questions.explanation: An internal (procedural) quality control is built into a testing device or test strip to verify that adequate sample volume was added and that reagents migrated properly (such as a control line color change on an automated or point-of-care cassette). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 66; PDF p. 91).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: What steps are taken when the results of reagent strip QC are outside the stated confidence limits?
choices: Check the expiration date of the reagent strip
Open a new reagent strips container
questions.explanation: When control values exceed established tolerance limits (out of control), patient results must not be reported. The technologist must verify control and reagent expiration dates, ensure proper mixing, retest with a fresh aliquot, and if still out of range, open a new vial of control or reagent lot and document all corrective actions. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book pp. 66–67; PDF pp. 91–92).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: When a new bottle of QC material is opened, what information is placed on the label?
choices: The date and the laboratory worker’s initials
The time the bottle was opened
questions.officialAnswer: The date and the laboratory worker’s initials
questions.explanation: Good laboratory practices and CLIA guidelines require that whenever a new vial of control material or reagent strip bottle is opened, the technologist must clearly write the date opened and their initials on the container label to verify active in-use expiration dates. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book p. 66; PDF p. 91).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: When a control is run, what information is documented?
questions.explanation: Comprehensive quality control documentation requires recording the reagent/control lot number, expiration date, analytical results, date, time, and operator initials on official QC logsheets or laboratory information systems to maintain regulatory compliance and traceability. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 1, Book pp. 66–67; PDF pp. 91–92).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: The principle commonly used to measure the concentration of a particular analyte in the chemical examination of urine is:
questions.explanation: Semiautomated and fully automated urine chemistry analyzers utilize reflectance photometry to quantify color changes on reagent strip test pads. Light of specific wavelengths strikes the reagent pad, and the intensity of light reflected from the pad is measured by a photodetector; reflectance is inversely related to color intensity and analyte concentration. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 76; PDF p. 101).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: In automated urinalysis, the specific gravity is measured by:
questions.explanation: Automated urine analyzers measure specific gravity using an integrated optical refractometer or refractive index module rather than reagent pad color changes or urinometry, ensuring high precision and temperature-corrected measurements across wide concentration ranges. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 77; PDF p. 102).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: All of the following are true concerning fully automated urine chemistry analyzers, except:
choices: They are designed for a high-volume urinalysis laboratory.
The reagent strip is dipped into the well-mixed urine.
The urine tube moves through the instrument.
A sample probe aspirates the urine.
questions.officialAnswer: The reagent strip is dipped into the well-mixed urine.
questions.explanation: Fully automated urine chemistry analyzers aspirate a precise volume of well-mixed urine via an automated sample probe and drop-dispense it onto each test pad individually. They do not immerse or dip the whole reagent strip into the urine tube, which prevents leaching of reagents between adjacent pads and avoids specimen cross-contamination. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 78; PDF p. 103).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: The advantages of an automated urine microscopy analyzer over manual microscopy includes:
questions.explanation: Automated urine microscopy systems offer substantial advantages over manual hemocytometer or glass-slide examination: they eliminate manual centrifugation and decanting steps, reduce labor costs, eliminate optical subjectivity, and standardize sediment concentration and volume per field examined. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 79; PDF p. 104).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a complete urinalysis automated urinalysis system?
questions.explanation: The Clinitek AUWi Pro System is an integrated, fully automated urinalysis workstation that combines automated reflectance chemistry testing (Clinitek Novus) with automated flow-cytometric urine particle analysis (Sysmex UF-1000i) on a shared specimen track. The AUTION ELEVEN and Clinitek Atlas perform chemistry only, and the standalone iQ200 performs microscopy only. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 81; PDF p. 106).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: What two technologies are used for urine sediment analysis?
questions.explanation: Modern automated urine microscopy instruments utilize two primary analytical technologies: planar digital imaging with auto particle recognition (APR) software (e.g., Iris iQ200/iRICELL) and fluorescent laser flow cytometry with electrical impedance/forward scatter (e.g., Sysmex UF series). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 79; PDF p. 104).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: Which automated urine particle counter combines urine flow cytometry with digital image analysis?
questions.explanation: The Sysmex UN-2000 workstation combines fluorescent flow cytometry (UF-5000) for initial cell/particle counting and categorization with an automated digital imaging unit (UD-10) to visually photograph and classify flagged sediment particles. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 83; PDF p. 108).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: Which of the following urine sediment particles cannot be autovalidated but will be flagged and must be reviewed by laboratory personnel?
questions.explanation: Renal tubular epithelial (RTE) cells carry high clinical significance (indicating acute tubular necrosis or renal graft rejection) and often share size/morphology overlap with transitional cells or small round cells. Auto-validation rules require instrument flags for RTEs, pathological casts, and unclassified elements to be verified by a technologist. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 84; PDF p. 109).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: Which of the automated body fluid analyzers does not need to dilute or pretreat body fluids before analysis?
questions.explanation: The Sysmex XN Series hematology analyzer features a dedicated body fluid software and aspiration mode that analyzes CSF, serous fluids, and synovial fluids directly from primary tubes without requiring manual pre-dilution or hyaluronidase pretreatment. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 86; PDF p. 111).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.subtopic: Urine and Body Fluid Analysis Automation
questions.prompt: What is a disadvantage of counting body fluid cells using an automated instrument versus a Neubauer hemocytometer?
choices: Unable to count low WBC numbers and malignant cells
Able to perform a WBC differential
questions.officialAnswer: Unable to count low WBC numbers and malignant cells
questions.explanation: While automated body fluid analyzers provide rapid, precise counts on clear fluids, their primary clinical disadvantages compared with manual hemocytometer/cytocentrifuge preparations include lower sensitivity at very low cell counts (e.g., normal CSF with 0–5 WBCs/uL) and inability to detect or definitively identify malignant cells, blast forms, or intracellular bacteria. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 87; PDF p. 112).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The primary inorganic substance found in urine is:
questions.explanation: Chloride is the principal inorganic solute excreted in normal urine, followed closely by sodium and potassium. Urea and creatinine are the major organic solutes. Phosphate and sulfate are present in smaller inorganic fractions. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 94; PDF p. 119).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An unidentified fluid is received in the laboratory with a request to determine whether the fluid is urine or another body fluid. Using routine laboratory tests, which substances would determine that the fluid is most probably urine?
questions.explanation: When a suspicious body fluid or drainage specimen (e.g., from an accidental bladder puncture or ruptured amniotic sac) is received, testing for urea nitrogen and creatinine provides positive differentiation. Normal urine contains concentrations of urea and creatinine many times higher than serum or other extravascular body fluids. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 94; PDF p. 119).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The average daily output of urine is:
questions.explanation: Under normal physiological hydration and diet, average adult daily urine output is 1200 to 1500 mL in 24 hours, though 600 to 2000 mL is considered physiological depending on fluid consumption and ambient climate. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 95; PDF p. 120).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A patient presenting with polyuria, nocturia, polydipsia, and a low urine specific gravity is exhibiting symptoms of:
questions.explanation: A patient with polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, and a dilute, low specific gravity (often < 1.005) presents classic signs of diabetes insipidus (caused by inadequate vasopressin/ADH secretion or renal tubular unresponsiveness). Conversely, diabetes mellitus produces polyuria with elevated specific gravity driven by osmotic diuresis from heavy glucose excretion. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 95; PDF p. 120).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A patient with oliguria might progress to having:
questions.explanation: Oliguria (urine output < 400 mL/day in adults) denotes significant renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury and can progress directly to anuria (complete absence of urine production, < 50 mL/day), indicating severe bilateral renal failure or complete urinary tract obstruction. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 95; PDF p. 120).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are characteristics of recommended urine containers except:
questions.explanation: Standard routine urine specimen containers must feature a wide opening (minimum 4–5 cm diameter), a flat stable base to avoid accidental tipping, clear inert plastic walls, and a secure leak-resistant screw-cap. Round or pointed conical bottoms tip over easily and are unacceptable. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 96; PDF p. 121).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Labels for urine containers are:
choices: Placed on the container before collection
questions.officialAnswer: Placed on the container before collection
questions.explanation: Specimen identification labels must be placed directly onto the wall of the urine container, never on the lid. Lids are detached during analysis and can easily be swapped or misplaced, causing critical specimen identification errors. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 96; PDF p. 121).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A urine specimen may be rejected by the laboratory for all of the following reasons except the fact that the:
choices: Requisition form states the specimen is catheterized
Label and requisition form do not match
Outside of the container has contamination from fecal material
questions.officialAnswer: Requisition form states the specimen is catheterized
questions.explanation: A urine specimen collected in a sterile screw-top container is fully acceptable for routine urinalysis. Laboratories reject specimens for missing/mismatched labels, external leakage, improper preservation, insufficient volume, or prolonged room temperature transit time exceeding 2 hours. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 96; PDF p. 121).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A cloudy specimen received in the laboratory may have been preserved using:
questions.explanation: Refrigeration at 2°C to 8°C preserves chemical analytes and prevents bacterial multiplication, but cold temperatures decrease solubility of physiological salts, resulting in cloudiness from amorphous urates (pinkish precipitate in acid urine) or amorphous phosphates (white precipitate in alkaline urine). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 97; PDF p. 122).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: For general screening, the specimen collected most frequently is a:
questions.explanation: Random spot urine specimens can be voided at any time of day and are the most convenient and routinely requested specimens for general outpatient health screening and acute hospital admissions. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 98; PDF p. 123).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The primary advantage of a first morning specimen over a random specimen is that it:
questions.explanation: A first morning specimen (voided immediately upon waking after overnight bladder incubation) is the most concentrated, acidic specimen of the day. Its high concentration prevents false-negative pregnancy tests and ensures preservation of casts and cellular constituents that might lyse in dilute daytime specimens. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 98; PDF p. 123).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: If a routine urinalysis and a culture are requested on a catheterized specimen, then:
choices: Two separate containers must be collected
The routine urinalysis is performed first
questions.explanation: When a single clean-catch or catheterized specimen arrives for both urinalysis and microbiological culture, the sterile urine culture aliquot must be set up or preserved first before opening the tube for reagent strip dipping or unsterile urinalysis handling, preventing introduced bacterial contamination. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 98; PDF p. 123).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: If a patient fails to discard the first specimen when collecting a timed specimen, then the:
questions.explanation: A proper 24-hour collection requires voiding and discarding the first morning specimen on Day 1 (to begin with an empty bladder at time zero) and collecting all subsequent urine including the first void of Day 2. If the initial morning specimen is mistakenly included, the container contains more than 24 hours of solute excretion, yielding falsely elevated volume and analyte clearance values. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 99; PDF p. 124).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The primary cause of unsatisfactory results in an unpreserved routine specimen not tested for 8 hours is:
questions.explanation: The clean-catch midstream collection technique is designed to obtain bladder urine free of urethral, vaginal, and skin flora. The primary cause of contaminated, unsatisfactory results (high squamous epithelial cell count and mixed bacteria) is failure of the patient to properly cleanse external genitalia or to void the initial stream before collecting the midstream portion. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 98; PDF p. 123).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Prolonged exposure of a preserved urine specimen to light will cause:
questions.explanation: Bilirubin molecules are highly photosensitive; when a urine specimen is exposed to fluorescent or sunlight, conjugated bilirubin is rapidly oxidized to biliverdin, which does not react with the diazonium salt on the bilirubin reagent test pad, resulting in false-negative results. Urobilinogen is also oxidized to urobilin. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 97; PDF p. 122).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be least affected in a specimen that has remained unpreserved at room temperature for more than 2 hours?
questions.explanation: While cells and casts lyse in dilute or alkaline urine, glucose is metabolized by bacteria, and bilirubin is oxidized by light, urinary protein (primarily albumin) is relatively stable over time at room temperature compared to the other labile urinalysis constituents. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 97; PDF p. 122).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Bacterial growth in an unpreserved specimen will:
questions.explanation: In unpreserved specimens standing at room temperature, multiplying urease-producing bacteria (such as Proteus mirabilis) hydrolyze urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, which alkalinizes the specimen and elevates pH (frequently > 8.0). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 97; PDF p. 122).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The most sterile specimen collected is a:
questions.explanation: Suprapubic needle aspiration (percutaneous needle puncture directly through the abdominal wall into the distended bladder) provides the purest, most sterile urine sample. It completely avoids urethral, vaginal, and perineal contamination and is ideal for anaerobic bacterial cultures and infants. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 99; PDF p. 124).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following would not be given to a patient before the collection of a midstream clean-catch specimen?
questions.explanation: For infants and non-toilet-trained children, specialized sterile hypoallergenic plastic collection bags with adhesive perianal seals are applied; bedpans are intended for bedridden adults and cannot capture uncontaminated pediatric voids. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 99; PDF p. 124).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Urine specimen collection for drug testing requires the collector to do all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Urine specimens collected for medical-legal, forensic, or employment drug screening must maintain a strict, uninterrupted chain-of-custody (COC) protocol. This includes observed collection, temperature verification (32.5°C to 37.7°C within 4 minutes), tamper-evident sealing, and documented chronological transfer logs. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 100; PDF p. 125).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The type of nephron responsible for renal concentration is the:
questions.explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons account for approximately 15% of nephrons and possess long loops of Henle that extend deep into the hypertonic renal medulla; their primary physiological function is establishing and maintaining the osmotic gradient required for urine concentration. Cortical nephrons (85%) have short loops and function primarily in solute reabsorption and secretion. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 106; PDF p. 131).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The function of the peritubular capillaries is:
questions.explanation: The peritubular capillaries arise from the efferent arteriole and surround the proximal and distal convoluted tubules. Their low hydrostatic pressure and high oncotic pressure favor the rapid reabsorption of filtered nutrients and fluid back into the systemic circulation, as well as the active tubular secretion of metabolic waste products. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 106; PDF p. 131).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Blood flows through the nephron in the following order:
choices: Efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries, vasa recta, afferent arteriole
Peritubular capillaries, afferent arteriole, vasa recta, efferent arteriole
Afferent arteriole, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries, vasa recta
Efferent arteriole, vasa recta, peritubular capillaries, afferent arteriole
questions.officialAnswer: Afferent arteriole, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries, vasa recta
questions.explanation: Blood enters the kidney via the renal artery, branches into interlobar, arcuate, and interlobular arteries, and enters the nephron through the afferent arteriole into the capillary tuft of the glomerulus. It exits the glomerulus via the narrower efferent arteriole, passes into the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta, and leaves via the renal vein. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 106; PDF p. 131).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Filtration of protein is prevented in the glomerulus by:
questions.explanation: Filtration of plasma albumin and larger macromolecules is prevented by the glomerular filtration barrier: capillary endothelial fenestrations, the negatively charged trilaminar glomerular basement membrane (heparan sulfate shield), and the visceral epithelial podocytes with foot processes and slit diaphragms. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 108; PDF p. 133).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system is responsible for all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) regulates plasma sodium concentration, arterial blood pressure, and glomerular filtration rate. A drop in blood pressure or sodium is sensed by the macula densa and juxtaglomerular cells, initiating renin release to generate angiotensin II and aldosterone. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 107; PDF p. 132).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The primary chemical affected by the renin–angiotensin– aldosterone system is:
questions.explanation: The primary chemical constituent that regulates the RAAS cascade is sodium. When the macula densa cells in the distal tubule detect decreased sodium chloride delivery, they signal the juxtaglomerular cells to secrete renin into the bloodstream. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 107; PDF p. 132).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Secretion of renin is stimulated by:
questions.explanation: Secretion of renin by the juxtaglomerular cells is stimulated by decreased arterial blood pressure, decreased renal perfusion pressure, reduced blood volume, or decreased sodium concentration reaching the macula densa. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 107; PDF p. 132).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The hormone aldosterone is responsible for:
questions.explanation: The mineralocorticoid hormone aldosterone, synthesized and secreted by the adrenal cortex, acts on the distal convoluted tubules and cortical collecting ducts to promote active sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion, retaining water and elevating systemic blood pressure. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 108; PDF p. 133).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The fluid leaving the glomerulus has a specific gravity of:
questions.explanation: The glomerular ultrafiltrate entering Bowman's capsule is essentially protein-free plasma with a fixed specific gravity of 1.010 (isosthenuric). As it traverses the tubules, cellular reabsorption and secretion modify its specific gravity between 1.002 and 1.035. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 108; PDF p. 133).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: For active transport to occur, a chemical must:
choices: Combine with a carrier protein to create electrochemical energy
Be filtered through the proximal convoluted tubule
Be in higher concentration in the filtrate than in the blood
Be in higher concentration in the blood than in the filtrate
questions.officialAnswer: Combine with a carrier protein to create electrochemical energy
questions.explanation: For active tubular transport to occur, the substance must combine with a specific membrane carrier protein that transfers it across cell membranes against an electrical or chemical concentration gradient, utilizing metabolic energy derived from ATP hydrolysis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 109; PDF p. 134).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the tubules is impermeable to water?
questions.explanation: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle (both thin and thick segments) is completely impermeable to water. The thick ascending limb actively pumps chloride and reabsorbs sodium into the medullary interstitium, diluting the luminal filtrate and creating the hypertonic medullary gradient. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 110; PDF p. 135).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Glucose will appear in the urine when the:
choices: Blood level of glucose is 200 mg/dL
Renal threshold for glucose is exceeded
questions.explanation: Glucose is normally completely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule by active transport. When plasma glucose exceeds the renal tubular transport maximum (Tm), which corresponds to a plasma concentration of 160 to 180 mg/dL, carrier proteins saturate and excess glucose spills into the urine (glucosuria). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 110; PDF p. 135).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Concentration of the tubular filtrate by the countercurrent mechanism depends on all of the following except:
choices: High salt concentration in the medulla
Water-impermeable walls of the ascending loop of Henle
Reabsorption of sodium and chloride from the ascending loop of Henle
Reabsorption of water in the descending loop of Henle
questions.officialAnswer: Reabsorption of water in the descending loop of Henle
questions.explanation: The countercurrent multiplier system relies on the opposing directions of filtrate flow within the descending and ascending limbs of the loops of Henle of juxtamedullary nephrons, coupled with countercurrent exchange in the parallel vasa recta capillary loops, maintaining high medullary osmolality. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 110; PDF p. 135).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: ADH regulates the final urine concentration by controlling:
questions.explanation: ADH (arginine vasopressin), released from the posterior pituitary, binds to V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells to insert aquaporin-2 water channels into the luminal membrane. This makes collecting duct epithelium permeable to water, allowing water to exit into the hypertonic medulla and concentrating the urine. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 111; PDF p. 136).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Decreased production of ADH:
choices: Produces a low volume of urine
Produces a high volume of urine
questions.officialAnswer: Produces a high volume of urine
questions.explanation: When ADH secretion is deficient (as in central diabetes insipidus), collecting duct walls remain impermeable to water. Tubular fluid cannot be reabsorbed, producing high-volume, hyposthenuric urine (polyuria). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 111; PDF p. 136).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Bicarbonate ions filtered by the glomerulus are returned to the blood:
questions.explanation: Filtered bicarbonate (HCO3-) cannot cross the luminal tubular membrane directly. Tubular cells secrete H+ ions, which combine with luminal HCO3- via brush-border carbonic anhydrase to form H2CO3, dissociating into CO2 and H2O. CO2 diffuses into tubular cells, regenerates HCO3-, and is returned to peritubular capillary blood. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 112; PDF p. 137).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: If ammonia is not produced by the distal convoluted tubule, the urine pH will be:
questions.explanation: Metabolic acid excretion requires tubular ammonia production (deamination of glutamine). If ammonia is not synthesized by the distal tubule cells, the minimum urinary pH limit (approx 4.5) is quickly reached, blocking further H+ secretion and impairing net acid excretion (type 1 distal renal tubular acidosis). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 112; PDF p. 137).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt:
Place the appropriate letter in front of the following clearance substances:
A. Exogenous
B. Endogenous

1. Beta2-microglobulin
2. Creatinine
3. Cystatin C
4. 125I-iothalamate
questions.officialAnswer: B: Beta2- microglobulin; B: Creatinine; B: Cystatin C; A: 125I- iodothalamate
questions.explanation: Endogenous clearance markers are naturally synthesized within the body: beta2-microglobulin (produced by nucleated cells), creatinine (from muscle phosphocreatine), and cystatin C (cysteine protease inhibitor). Exogenous markers must be administered intravenously: 125I-iothalamate and inulin. Mapping: B: Beta2-microglobulin; B: Creatinine; B: Cystatin C; A: 125I-iodothalamate. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book pp. 113–115; PDF pp. 138–140).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The largest source of error in creatinine clearance tests is:
questions.explanation: In creatinine clearance testing, the single greatest source of preanalytical error is inaccurate timing or incomplete collection of the timed (usually 24-hour) urine volume. Failure to collect all voids or inaccurate recording of collection duration invalidates the calculated clearance volume V (mL/min). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 114; PDF p. 139).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt:
Given the following information, calculate the creatinine clearance:

24-hour urine volume: 1000 mL; serum creatinine: 2.0 mg/dL; urine creatinine: 200 mg/dL
questions.explanation: Creatinine clearance C = (U * V) / P. Here, 24-hr urine volume = 1000 mL, so V = 1000 mL / 1440 min = 0.694 mL/min. Urine creatinine U = 200 mg/dL, and serum creatinine P = 2.0 mg/dL. C = (200 * 0.694) / 2.0 = 138.8 / 2.0 = 69.4 mL/min, rounding to 69 mL/min. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 114; PDF p. 139).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Clearance tests used to determine the glomerular filtration rate must measure substances that are:
choices: Completely reabsorbed by the proximal convoluted tubule
Secreted in the distal convoluted tubule
Neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules
questions.officialAnswer: Neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules
questions.explanation: Normal adult creatinine clearance reference ranges are 107 to 139 mL/min for men and 87 to 107 mL/min for women, reflecting differences in total skeletal muscle mass. Values decrease progressively with advancing age. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 114; PDF p. 139).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Performing a clearance test using radionucleotides:
choices: Eliminates the need to collect urine
questions.explanation: Infusion of radiolabeled pharmaceuticals such as 125I-iothalamate or 99mTc-DTPA enables highly precise assessment of GFR, and when combined with scintigraphic gamma-camera imaging, allows differential measurement of filtration rates in each kidney independently. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 115; PDF p. 140).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Variables that are included in the MDRD-IDSM estimated calculations of creatinine clearance include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) study equation for estimating GFR (eGFR) requires four patient variables: serum creatinine, chronological age, gender, and ethnicity (African American vs non-African American). It does not require height, body weight, or 24-hour urine collection. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 115; PDF p. 140).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An advantage to using cystatin C to monitor GFR is that:
choices: It does not require urine collection
It is not secreted by the tubules
It can be measured by immunoassay
questions.explanation: Serum cystatin C is a low-molecular-weight protein produced at a constant rate by all nucleated cells. It is freely filtered by the glomerulus and completely catabolized by proximal tubular cells. Its primary diagnostic advantage over creatinine is that circulating concentrations are independent of muscle mass, gender, race, and dietary meat intake. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 115; PDF p. 140).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Solute dissolved in solvent will:
questions.explanation: Adding solute particles to a pure solvent alters its four colligative properties: it depresses the freezing point, lowers the vapor pressure, elevates the boiling point, and increases the osmotic pressure proportional to the number of dissolved particles. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 117; PDF p. 142).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Substances that may interfere with freezing-point measurement of urine and serum osmolarity include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Volatile solutes such as ethanol, methanol, or isopropanol rapidly evaporate, interfering with vapor-pressure osmometry (yielding false normal values). Freezing-point depression osmometry measures all dissolved particles, including volatile alcohols. Lipids and particulate matter do not dissolve and do not alter freezing point. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 117; PDF p. 142).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Clinical osmometers use NaCl as a reference solution because:
choices: 1 g molecular weight of NaCl will lower the freezing point 1.86°C
NaCl is partially ionized, similar to the composition of urine
1 g equivalent weight of NaCl will raise the freezing point 1.86°C
questions.officialAnswer: NaCl is partially ionized, similar to the composition of urine
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride (NaCl) solutions of precisely known molality are universally employed as reference calibration standards in clinical osmometers because NaCl dissociates into ions with osmotic activity that closely mimics physiological serum and urine electrolytes. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 117; PDF p. 142).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The normal serum osmolarity is:
questions.explanation: Normal human serum osmolality is tightly regulated by hypothalamic osmoreceptors and ADH release within a narrow physiological reference range of 275 to 295 mOsm/kg. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 118; PDF p. 143).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: After controlled fluid intake, the urine-to-serum osmolarity ratio should be at least:
questions.explanation: Under random physiological conditions, normal urine-to-serum (U:S) osmolality ratio is at least 1:1. Following controlled fluid deprivation (water restriction for 12–16 hours), a functioning kidney concentrates urine to achieve a U:S ratio of at least 3:1 (urine osmolality >= 800 mOsm/kg). Note: The textbook answer key designates A (1:1), which reflects baseline random hydration, whereas textbook narrative on p. 118 notes that following controlled fluid restriction it should reach 3:1 (C). Official answer A is preserved. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 118; PDF p. 143; Answer Key p. 372/397).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt:
Calculate the free water clearance from the following results:

urine volume in 6 hours: 720 mL; urine osmolarity: 225 mOsm; plasma osmolarity: 300 mOsm
questions.explanation: Free water clearance formula: CH2O = V - Cosm. Given urine volume of 720 mL in 6 hours: V = 720 mL / (6 * 60 min) = 720 / 360 = 2.0 mL/min. Cosm = (U_osm * V) / P_osm = (225 * 2.0) / 300 = 450 / 300 = 1.5 mL/min. Therefore, CH2O = 2.0 - 1.5 = +0.5 mL/min. A positive value indicates hyposthenuric urine with excretion of excess water. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 118; PDF p. 143).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: To provide an accurate measure of renal blood flow, a test substance should be completely:
choices: Secreted when it reaches the distal convoluted tubule
Cleared on each contact with functional renal tissue
questions.officialAnswer: Cleared on each contact with functional renal tissue
questions.explanation: An ideal substance for measuring effective renal plasma flow (ERPF) and renal blood flow, such as p-aminohippuric acid (PAH), must be completely removed from plasma during a single transit through functional renal tissue (filtered by glomeruli and actively secreted by peritubular capillaries without reabsorption). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 119; PDF p. 144).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt:
Given the following data, calculate the effective renal plasma flow:

urine volume in 2 hours: 240 mL; urine PAH: 150 mg/dL; plasma PAH: 0.5 mg/dL
questions.explanation: Effective renal plasma flow (ERPF) is calculated using PAH clearance: ERPF = (U_PAH * V) / P_PAH. Urine volume in 2 hours = 240 mL, so V = 240 mL / (2 * 60 min) = 240 / 120 = 2.0 mL/min. U_PAH = 150 mg/dL, and P_PAH = 0.5 mg/dL. ERPF = (150 * 2.0) / 0.5 = 300 / 0.5 = 600 mL/min. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 119; PDF p. 144).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Renal tubular acidosis can be caused by the:
choices: Production of excessively acidic urine due to increased filtration of hydrogen ions
Production of excessively acidic urine due to increased secretion of hydrogen ions
Inability to produce an acidic urine due to impaired production of ammonia
Inability to produce an acidic urine due to increased production of ammonia
questions.officialAnswer: Inability to produce an acidic urine due to impaired production of ammonia
questions.explanation: Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) is characterized by systemic metabolic acidosis accompanied by an inability of the renal tubules to produce sufficiently acidic urine (urine pH remains > 5.5). This occurs either through impaired proximal bicarbonate reabsorption (Type 2) or impaired distal tubular hydrogen ion secretion and ammonia generation (Type 1). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 119; PDF p. 144).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Tests performed to detect renal tubular acidosis after administering an ammonium chloride load include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Following oral administration of an ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) acid load, tubular acidifying capacity is tested by analyzing urinary parameters over several hours: urine pH (which should fall below 5.3 in healthy individuals), titratable acidity, and urinary ammonia excretion. Arterial pH is not measured as part of this urinary acidification protocol. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 119; PDF p. 144).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The concentration of a normal urine specimen can be estimated by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Visual inspection of urine color provides an immediate rough assessment of urine concentration: dilute urine is pale straw or colorless, normal concentrated urine is yellow to amber, and highly concentrated urine (such as after fluid restriction or fever) is dark amber. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 126; PDF p. 151).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The normal yellow color of urine is produced by:
questions.explanation: Urochrome is the primary endogenous pigment imparting the characteristic yellow color to urine. It is excreted at a constant metabolic rate proportional to the body's basal metabolism; urobilin and uroerythrin are minor secondary pigments present in smaller amounts. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 126; PDF p. 151).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The presence of bilirubin in a urine specimen produces a:
questions.explanation: Urine containing conjugated bilirubin exhibits a dark amber or yellow-orange color and produces characteristic stable yellow foam when shaken. Normal urine or urine with elevated protein produces white foam; only bilirubin produces vivid yellow foam. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 127; PDF p. 152).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A urine specimen containing melanin will appear:
questions.explanation: In patients with malignant melanoma, colorless melanogen is excreted in urine and is oxidized by atmospheric oxygen upon standing, turning the urine dark brown or black. Homogentisic acid (alkaptonuria) also turns black upon standing in alkaline urine. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 128; PDF p. 153).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Specimens that contain hemoglobin can be visually distinguished from those that contain RBCs because:
choices: Hemoglobin produces a clear yellow specimen
Hemoglobin produces a cloudy pink specimen
RBCs produce a cloudy red specimen
RBCs produce a clear red specimen
questions.officialAnswer: RBCs produce a cloudy red specimen
questions.explanation: Both hemoglobin and myoglobin cause clear red or reddish-brown urine and positive reagent strip blood tests. They are distinguished visually by examining patient plasma: intravascular hemolysis releases free hemoglobin that binds haptoglobin and discolors plasma pink or red; myoglobin is cleared so rapidly by glomerular filtration that plasma remains clear and normal in color. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 127; PDF p. 152).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A patient with a viscous orange specimen may have been:
choices: Treated for a urinary tract infection
questions.officialAnswer: Treated for a urinary tract infection
questions.explanation: Phenazopyridine (Pyridium or Azo-Standard), an azo dye analgesic commonly prescribed for urinary tract pain and dysuria, imparts a dense bright orange color and viscous consistency to urine that interferes with spectrophotometric reagent strip readings. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 127; PDF p. 152).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The presence of a pink precipitate in a refrigerated specimen is caused by:
questions.explanation: Refrigeration of acidic urine causes precipitation of amorphous urate salts. The pink pigment uroerythrin binds to the surface of the urate granules, producing a macroscopic pink precipitate classically termed 'brick dust'. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 128; PDF p. 153).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Microscopic examination of a clear urine that produces a white precipitate after refrigeration will show:
questions.explanation: Microscopic analysis of the refrigerated pink precipitate reveals nonpathologic, granular amorphous urate crystals. They dissolve readily upon gentle warming to 60°C or addition of dilute sodium hydroxide. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 128; PDF p. 153).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The color of urine containing porphyrins will be:
questions.explanation: Excessive excretion of porphyrins (in congenital erythropoietic porphyria or porphyria cutanea tarda) imparts a classic 'port wine' or dark burgundy red color to urine that intensifies after oxidation by light and air. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 128; PDF p. 153).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following specific gravities would be most likely to correlate with a urine that is pale yellow?
questions.explanation: Pale yellow, nearly colorless urine is associated with high fluid intake and low solute concentration, typically exhibiting a specific gravity around 1.005. Dark amber urine correlates with high specific gravities (>= 1.030). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 129; PDF p. 154).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A urine specific gravity measured by a refractometer is 1.029, and the temperature of the urine is 14°C. The specific gravity should be reported as:
questions.explanation: A clinical refractometer measures the refractive index of light through urine compared with distilled water; the angle of refraction is directly proportional to the total concentration of dissolved solute particles in the solution. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 130; PDF p. 155).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The principle of refractive index is to compare:
choices: Light velocity in solutions with light velocity in solids
Light velocity in air with light velocity in solutions
Light scattering by air with light scattering by solutions
Light scattering by particles in solution
questions.officialAnswer: Light velocity in air with light velocity in solutions
questions.explanation: Refractive index (n) is defined physically as the velocity of light in air divided by the velocity of light in the test solution. As dissolved solute concentration increases, light travels more slowly, increasing the angle of refraction. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 130; PDF p. 155).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A correlation exists between a specific gravity by a refractometer of 1.050 and a:
questions.explanation: Under physiological conditions without heavy radiographic contrast or high protein/glucose, refractometer specific gravity correlates well with total dissolved solids, freezing-point osmolality, and reagent strip polyelectrolyte pKa readings. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 131; PDF p. 156).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A cloudy urine specimen turns black upon standing and has a specific gravity of 1.012. The major concern about this specimen would be:
questions.explanation: In alkaptonuria (an inborn error of tyrosine metabolism lacking homogentisic acid oxidase), excreted homogentisic acid accumulates; when voided urine stands and becomes alkaline, the compound spontaneously oxidizes to a brownish-black pigment, testing negative for blood. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 128; PDF p. 153).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A specimen with a specific gravity of 1.035 would be considered:
questions.explanation: Urine with a specific gravity above 1.010 is hypersthenuric (more concentrated than the glomerular ultrafiltrate); exactly 1.010 is isosthenuric; and below 1.010 is hyposthenuric. A value of 1.035 represents hypersthenuric urine. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 129; PDF p. 154).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A specimen with a specific gravity of 1.001 would be considered:
questions.explanation: The human kidney cannot produce urine with a specific gravity lower than 1.002 to 1.003, even during maximal water diuresis. A reading of 1.001 or 1.000 indicates that the specimen is essentially water and suggests intentional specimen dilution or adulteration (such as in drug screening). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 129; PDF p. 154).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A strong odor of ammonia in a urine specimen could indicate:
questions.explanation: A pungent ammoniacal odor develops when unpreserved urine stands at room temperature as multiplying urease-producing bacteria hydrolyze urea into volatile ammonia gas. Freshly voided urine has only a faintly aromatic odor. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 132; PDF p. 157).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The microscopic examination of a clear red urine is reported as many WBCs and epithelial cells. What does this suggest?
choices: Possible mix-up of specimen and sediment
questions.officialAnswer: Possible mix-up of specimen and sediment
questions.explanation: When urine is clear red and chemical reagent strips are strongly positive for blood, but the microscopic examination demonstrates 0 RBCs/hpf, the color and reactivity are caused by free dissolved pigment—either hemoglobin (from intravascular hemolysis or in vitro RBC lysis) or myoglobin (from rhabdomyolysis). Hematuria produces cloudy/smoky red urine with intact RBCs. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 127; PDF p. 152).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following would contribute the most to a urine osmolality?
questions.explanation: Unlike osmolality (which depends solely on the number of dissolved particles), specific gravity is a density measurement that depends on both the number and the molecular mass of solute particles. Large high-molecular-weight molecules (such as radiographic contrast media, glucose, and protein) increase specific gravity disproportionately. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 129; PDF p. 154).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following colligative properties is not stated correctly?
choices: The boiling point is raised by solute
The freezing point is raised by solute
The vapor pressure is lowered by solute
The osmotic pressure is raised by solute
questions.officialAnswer: The freezing point is raised by solute
questions.explanation: Colligative properties depend exclusively on the number of dissolved particles in solution: freezing-point depression, vapor-pressure depression, boiling-point elevation, and osmotic pressure. Physical properties such as color, viscosity, and volume are non-colligative. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 131; PDF p. 156).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An osmole contains:
choices: One gram molecular weight of solute dissolved in 1 liter of solvent
One gram molecular weight of solute dissolved in 1 kilogram of solvent
Two gram molecular weights of solute dissolved in 1 liter of solvent
Two gram molecular weights of solute dissolved in 1 kilogram of solvent
questions.officialAnswer: One gram molecular weight of solute dissolved in 1 kilogram of solvent
questions.explanation: An osmole (Osm) is defined as 1 gram molecular weight (1 mole) of an un-ionized solute, or 1 mole divided by the number of dissociable ions (particles) in solution, representing 1 mole of osmotically active particles (6.02 x 10^23 particles). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 131; PDF p. 156).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The unit of osmolality measured in the clinical laboratory is the:
questions.explanation: In clinical medicine, osmotic concentration is routinely expressed as osmolality in milliosmoles per kilogram of water (mOsm/kg), because mass (unlike volume in osmolarity) is temperature-independent. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 131; PDF p. 156).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: In the reagent strip specific gravity reaction, the polyelectrolyte:
choices: Combines with hydrogen ions in response to ion concentration
Releases hydrogen ions in response to ion concentration
Releases hydrogen ions in response to pH
Combines with sodium ions in response to pH
questions.officialAnswer: Releases hydrogen ions in response to ion concentration
questions.explanation: The reagent strip test for specific gravity contains a pre-treated polyelectrolyte (poly(methyl vinyl ether/maleic anhydride)). Cations in the urine (primarily Na+, K+, NH4+) exchange with hydrogen ions on the polyelectrolyte, releasing H+ ions and lowering pH. The bromthymol blue pH indicator changes from blue-green (low ionic strength) to yellow-green (high ionic strength). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 131; PDF p. 156).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following will react in the reagent strip specific gravity test?
questions.explanation: Because the reagent strip reaction relies exclusively on ion exchange with a polyelectrolyte, it measures only ionic solutes (electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, chloride, and ammonium). Non-ionized solutes—including glucose, urea, and radiographic contrast media—do not release hydrogen ions and do not elevate reagent strip specific gravity. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 5, Book p. 131; PDF p. 156).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Leaving excess urine on the reagent strip after removing it from the specimen will:
choices: Alter the color of the specimen
Cause reagents to leach from the pads
questions.explanation: Leaving excess urine on the reagent strip causes 'runover' between adjacent chemical pads, mixing contrasting buffer reagents (such as the acid buffer from the protein pad washing onto the pH pad) and producing distorted, erroneous color reactions. Excess urine should be blotted against the edge of the container or an absorbent pad. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 6, Book p. 140; PDF p. 165).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Failure to mix a specimen before inserting the reagent strip will primarily affect the:
questions.explanation: Formed cellular constituents, including erythrocytes and leukocytes, rapidly settle to the bottom of the container. If the urine is not thoroughly mixed before immersing the reagent strip, test pads will contact cell-depleted supernatant, leading to false-negative or falsely low blood and leukocyte esterase results. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 6, Book p. 140; PDF p. 165).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Testing a refrigerated specimen that has not warmed to room temperature will adversely affect:
questions.explanation: Testing a refrigerated urine specimen that has not been allowed to equilibrate to room temperature causes false-negative or delayed reactions on pads that rely on enzymatic activity (such as glucose oxidase and leukocyte esterase), because low temperatures significantly impede enzymatic reaction kinetics. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 6, Book p. 140; PDF p. 165).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The reagent strip reaction that requires the longest reaction time is the:
questions.explanation: Reagent strip pads have specific incubation intervals: glucose and bilirubin are read at 30 seconds; ketones at 40; specific gravity at 45; pH, protein, blood, urobilinogen, and nitrite at 60 seconds; and leukocyte esterase requires a full 120 seconds (2 minutes) to reach peak color development. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 6, Book p. 140; PDF p. 165).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Quality control of reagent strips is performed:
questions.explanation: Clinical laboratory standards require testing positive and negative control solutions on reagent strips at least once every 24 hours (or at the beginning of each shift), whenever a new bottle or lot is opened, and whenever analytical results are in doubt or instrument calibration changes. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 6, Book p. 141; PDF p. 166).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are important to protect the integrity of reagent strips except:
choices: Removing the desiccant from the bottle
Resealing the bottle after removing a strip
questions.officialAnswer: Removing the desiccant from the bottle
questions.explanation: Reagent strips must be stored in their original opaque containers with desiccant at cool room temperature (below 30°C, typically 15°C–30°C). They should never be frozen or stored in refrigerators unless manufacturer-specified, as refrigeration causes condensation upon opening that degrades test pads. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 6, Book p. 140; PDF p. 165).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The principle of the reagent strip test for pH is the:
questions.explanation: The reagent strip pH pad employs a dual-indicator system combining methyl red (active range pH 4.4 to 6.2, changing red to yellow) and bromthymol blue (active range pH 6.0 to 7.6, changing yellow to blue).
