questions.explanation: CSF collected via lumbar puncture is distributed into three or four consecutively numbered sterile tubes: Tube 1 is delivered to Chemistry/Serology; Tube 2 to Microbiology; and Tube 3 to Hematology for cell counts and cytological differential, minimizing the effect of potential needle-puncture blood contamination. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 255; PDF p. 280).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The CSF tube that should be kept at room temperature is:
questions.explanation: Tube 2 (Microbiology) must be maintained at room temperature (22°C–25°C) because refrigeration is lethal to cold-sensitive, fastidious meningitis-causing pathogens such as Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae. Tube 1 (Chemistry) is frozen and Tube 3 (Hematology) is refrigerated. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 255; PDF p. 280).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt:
Place the appropriate letter in front of the statement that describes A. Traumatic tap or B. Intracranial hemorrhage:

1. Xanthochromic supernatant
2. Presence of erythrophages/siderophages
3. Decreasing blood in successive collection tubes
4. Clot formation in collection tube
questions.explanation: Differentiating cerebral hemorrhage (B) from traumatic puncture (A): Uneven blood distribution with clearing in successive tubes = A; Xanthochromic centrifuged supernatant = B; Clot formation due to fibrinogen = A; Absence of clotting and presence of hemosiderin/siderophages = B. Sequence: B, B, A, A. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 256–257; PDF pp. 281–282).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

items: Decreasing blood in successive collection tubes

questions.prompt: The presence of xanthochromia can be caused by all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Xanthochromia refers to a pink, orange, or yellow discoloration of the cell-free CSF supernatant. It is produced by breakdown of red blood cells into oxyhemoglobin (pink/orange) and bilirubin (yellow), severe systemic hyperbilirubinemia, or elevated protein > 150 mg/dL with bound pigments. Pure albumin without pigment does not impart xanthochromia. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 256; PDF p. 281).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A web-like pellicle in a refrigerated CSF specimen indicates:
questions.explanation: In tuberculous meningitis, high protein and fibrinogen content combined with low cell counts allows a fine, web-like fibrin clot or delicate surface 'pellicle' to form after 12 to 24 hours of undisturbed refrigeration. Acid-fast bacilli are often trapped within this pellicle. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 256; PDF p. 281).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Given the following information, calculate the CSF WBC count: cells counted, 80; dilution, 1:10; large Neubauer squares counted, 10.
questions.explanation: Standard hemocytometer calculation: Cells/uL = (Cells counted x Dilution) / (Area counted [mm2] x Depth [0.1 mm]). Using a standard Neubauer chamber counting all 9 large squares (0.9 uL total volume) or the 4 corner squares (0.4 uL), this standard formula yields the exact cell concentration per microliter. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 257–258; PDF pp. 282–283).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A CSF WBC count is diluted with:
questions.explanation: When performing manual WBC counts on bloody or hazy CSF, the specimen is diluted with a solution of 3% glacial acetic acid (which rapidly hemolyzes all non-nucleated erythrocytes) and gentian violet or methylene blue (which stains the nuclei of leukocytes), facilitating accurate differential counting. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 257; PDF p. 282).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A total CSF cell count on a clear fluid should be:
questions.explanation: Normal and completely clear CSF specimens contain very few cells (normal adult reference range: 0 to 5 WBCs/uL, 0 RBCs/uL). Diluting a clear specimen would make counting rare cells statistically invalid; clear fluids must therefore be mixed well and loaded directly undiluted into the hemocytometer. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 257; PDF p. 282).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The purpose of adding albumin to CSF before cytocentrifugation is to:
questions.explanation: Because CSF has extremely low baseline protein concentration, the high centrifugal forces of cytocentrifugation tend to flatten and rupture delicate leukocytes. Adding a drop of 22% or 30% albumin to the sample chamber increases fluid oncotic pressure, prevents mechanical distortion, and markedly increases cell recovery on the slide. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 258; PDF p. 283).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The primary concern when pleocytosis of neutrophils and lymphocytes is found in the CSF is:
questions.explanation: The immediate primary clinical concern when CSF cytocentrifugation demonstrates a marked neutrophilic pleocytosis (thousands of WBCs/uL, predominantly segmented neutrophils) is acute purulent bacterial meningitis, requiring emergency stat Gram stain, culture, and immediate intravenous antibiotic therapy. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 259; PDF p. 284).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Neutrophils with pyknotic nuclei may be mistaken for:
questions.explanation: In standing or infected CSF specimens, senescent neutrophils undergo nuclear pyknosis where the chromatin condenses into dark, spherical, homogenous nuclear masses that lose typical segmentation, resembling orthochromatic normoblasts (nucleated red blood cells). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 259; PDF p. 284).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The presence of which of the following cells is increased in a parasitic infection?
questions.explanation: An elevated lymphocyte and monocyte count (mononuclear pleocytosis) is the typical cytological finding in viral (aseptic) meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, fungal infections (Cryptococcus neoformans), neurosyphilis, and multiple sclerosis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 260; PDF p. 285).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Macrophages appear in the CSF after:
questions.explanation: Macrophages (monocytes that differentiate upon entering the subarachnoid space) appear in CSF within 2 to 4 hours following subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke, or invasive neurological procedures; they rapidly phagocytose extravasated erythrocytes (erythrophagocytosis) and lipid debris. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 261; PDF p. 286).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Nucleated RBCs are seen in the CSF as a result of:
questions.explanation: When the lumbar puncture needle accidentally strikes the vertebral body periosteum or enters vertebral bone marrow, immature hematopoietic precursors—including nucleated RBCs, myelocytes, and megakaryocytes—are aspirated into the CSF specimen. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 261; PDF p. 286).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: After a CNS diagnostic procedure, which of the following might be seen in the CSF?
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells (lining the ventricles and neural canal) and choroid plexus epithelial cells are nonpathologic lining cells that become mechanically dislodged and appear in clusters or sheets following neurosurgical manipulation, shunt placement, or pneumoencephalography. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 262; PDF p. 287).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Hemosiderin granules and hematoidin crystals are seen in:
questions.explanation: Following phagocytosis of RBCs by macrophages in subarachnoid hemorrhage, hemoglobin is metabolized into blue-black hemosiderin granules (Prussian blue positive) and iron-free, yellow-orange hematoidin crystals (crystalline bilirubin) within the macrophage cytoplasm. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 261; PDF p. 286).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Myeloblasts are seen in the CSF:
choices: As a complication of acute leukemia
questions.officialAnswer: As a complication of acute leukemia
questions.explanation: Leukemic blasts (myeloblasts or lymphoblasts) appear in the CSF when circulating leukemic cells cross the blood-brain barrier and seed the leptomeninges (meningeal leukemia), a frequent site of relapse in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 262; PDF p. 287).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Cells resembling large and small lymphocytes with cleaved nuclei represent:
questions.explanation: Metastatic or primary central nervous system lymphoma produces abnormal lymphoid cells that display atypical cytologic features: nuclear convolutions and clefting, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, irregular chromatin clumping, and prominent macronucleoli. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 263; PDF p. 288).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The reference range for CSF protein is:
questions.explanation: Normal adult CSF total protein concentration is extremely low compared with plasma (approximately 1/200th of serum levels), with a well-established reference interval of 15 to 45 mg/dL. Values are slightly higher in neonates and elderly adults. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 264; PDF p. 289).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: CSF can be differentiated from serum by the presence of:
questions.explanation: When analyzing fluid from suspected rhinorrhea or otorrhea to confirm CSF leakage following head trauma, protein electrophoresis or immunofixation identifies the unique carbohydrate-deficient isoform of transferrin ('tau' protein) and prominent prealbumin, which are characteristic of CSF and absent in serum or nasal secretions. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 264; PDF p. 289).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: In serum, the second most prevalent protein is IgG; in CSF, the second most prevalent protein is:
questions.explanation: On protein electrophoresis, albumin represents the largest fraction in both serum and CSF; however, prealbumin (transthyretin) is the second most prominent protein band in normal CSF, whereas in serum, immunoglobulins (IgG) and alpha-globulins are far more abundant. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 264; PDF p. 289).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Elevated values for CSF protein can be caused by all of the following except:
questions.explanation: CSF protein is elevated in meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, brain tumors, neurosyphilis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and multiple sclerosis due to increased BBB permeability or intrathecal synthesis. Systemic hypoproteinemia or water intoxication produces abnormally low CSF protein values (< 15 mg/dL). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 264; PDF p. 289).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The integrity of the blood–brain barrier is measured using the:
questions.explanation: Because albumin is synthesized exclusively in the liver and cannot be produced within the central nervous system, any albumin present in CSF must cross the blood-brain barrier. The CSF/serum albumin index = [CSF albumin (mg/dL) / Serum albumin (g/dL)]; an index < 9 represents an intact BBB, 9–14 slight impairment, 15–30 moderate impairment, and > 30 severe breakdown. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 265; PDF p. 290).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Given the following results, calculate the IgG index: CSF IgG, 50 mg/dL; serum IgG, 2 g/dL; CSF albumin, 70 mg/dL; serum albumin, 5 g/dL.
questions.explanation: The IgG index formula: IgG index = [CSF IgG (mg/dL) / Serum IgG (g/dL)] / [CSF albumin (mg/dL) / Serum albumin (g/dL)]. An index > 0.70 demonstrates intrathecal synthesis of IgG within the central nervous system. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 265; PDF p. 290).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The CSF IgG index calculated in Study Question 28 indicates:
choices: Synthesis of IgG in the CNS
questions.officialAnswer: Synthesis of IgG in the CNS
questions.explanation: An elevated CSF IgG index (> 0.70) indicates that local immunoglobulin production is occurring within the central nervous system by B lymphocytes, strongly supporting the clinical diagnosis of multiple sclerosis or other neuroinflammatory demyelinating diseases. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 265; PDF p. 290).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The finding of oligoclonal bands in the CSF and not in the serum is seen with:
questions.explanation: Isoelectric focusing (IEF) of CSF paired with serum demonstrates discrete 'oligoclonal bands' in the gamma zone in over 90% of patients with multiple sclerosis. To be clinically diagnostic, the bands must be present in the CSF and completely absent in simultaneous serum, verifying CNS-restricted synthesis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 265; PDF p. 290).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which condition is suggested by the following results: a CSF glucose of 15 mg/dL, WBC count of 5000, 90% neutrophils, and protein of 80 mg/dL?
questions.explanation: Myelin basic protein (MBP) is a component of the axonal myelin sheath. Elevated concentrations in CSF indicate active, ongoing demyelination and acute axonal breakdown, providing an objective biomarker to monitor acute relapse episodes in multiple sclerosis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 266; PDF p. 291).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A patient with a blood glucose of 120 mg/dL would have a normal CSF glucose of:
questions.explanation: Glucose enters the CSF by active transport and facilitated diffusion across the choroid plexus; under physiological equilibrium, normal CSF glucose concentration is 60% to 70% of the simultaneous plasma glucose. For a blood glucose of 120 mg/dL, normal expected CSF glucose is approximately 72 to 84 mg/dL. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 266; PDF p. 291).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: CSF lactate will be more consistently decreased in:
questions.explanation: In viral (aseptic) meningitis, cerebral oxygenation is maintained and tissue glycolysis is minimal, resulting in normal or lower CSF lactate levels (< 25 mg/dL). Conversely, tissue hypoxia and bacterial metabolism in purulent bacterial, fungal, or tubercular meningitis consistently drive lactate levels > 25–35 mg/dL. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 267; PDF p. 292).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Measurement of which of the following can be replaced by CSF glutamine analysis in children with Reye syndrome?
questions.explanation: Measuring CSF lactate levels provides rapid, highly sensitive clinical differentiation between bacterial and viral meningitis: values > 35 mg/dL strongly indicate bacterial infection, whereas viral meningitis rarely exceeds 25 mg/dL. It replaces older, more technically demanding methods such as CSF glutamine. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 267; PDF p. 292).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Before performing a Gram stain on CSF, the specimen must be:
questions.explanation: Because bacterial counts in early or partially treated meningitis may be relatively low, the CSF specimen must be concentrated by centrifugation (at 1500 RCF for 15 minutes) or cytocentrifugation, and the Gram stain smear prepared from the concentrated sediment button to maximize microscopic diagnostic yield. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 268; PDF p. 293).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following statements are true about cryptococcal meningitis except:
choices: An India ink preparation is positive
A starburst pattern is seen on Gram stain
A confirmatory immunology test is available
questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans is an opportunistic encapsulated yeast that causes fungal meningitis in immunocompromised patients; on classic negative India ink or nigrosin preparations, the thick gelatinous mucopolysaccharide capsule excludes colloidal ink particles, appearing as a prominent clear halo surrounding the budding yeast. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 268; PDF p. 293).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The most sensitive and specific method to detect the causative organism in meningitis is:
questions.explanation: Direct detection of cryptococcal capsular polysaccharide antigen (CrAg) using latex agglutination (LA) or lateral flow immunochromatography (LFA) has largely superseded India ink smears; CrAg testing provides over 95% to 98% clinical sensitivity and specificity and is the gold standard diagnostic method. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 269; PDF p. 294).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The test of choice to detect neurosyphilis is the:
questions.explanation: The Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) microflocculation test is the only CDC-approved and CLSI-recommended non-treponemal test for diagnosing neurosyphilis on cerebrospinal fluid. The Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) test cannot be used on CSF because it produces false-positive results. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 269; PDF p. 294).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Maturation of spermatozoa takes place in the:
questions.explanation: Spermatozoa are produced in the seminiferous tubules of the testes and then travel to the epididymis, where they mature, acquire progressive motility, and develop fertilization capacity over a period of 10 to 14 days. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 278; PDF p. 303).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Enzymes for the coagulation and liquefaction of semen are produced by the:
questions.explanation: Prostatic secretions (accounting for ~20%–30% of semen volume) contain acid phosphatase, citric acid, zinc, and proteolytic enzymes (including prostate-specific antigen, PSA) that are responsible for the enzymatic coagulation and subsequent liquefaction of the seminal coagulum. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 278; PDF p. 303).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The major component of seminal fluid is:
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles produce the largest portion of the seminal ejaculate (approximately 60%–70% of total volume), secreting high concentrations of fructose (the principal energy source for sperm motility) and flavin pigments responsible for normal grayish-white opalescence. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 278; PDF p. 303).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: If the first portion of a semen specimen is not collected, the semen analysis will have which of the following?
questions.explanation: During ejaculation, the initial fluid expelled consists of prostatic fluid containing the vast majority of spermatozoa, followed by seminal vesicle secretions. If the initial portion of the ejaculate is lost or missed, the measured sperm count and concentration will be falsely decreased, and pH will be falsely elevated. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 279; PDF p. 304).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Failure of laboratory personnel to document the time a semen specimen is collected primarily affects the interpretation of semen:
questions.explanation: Freshly ejaculated semen is clotted and must undergo liquefaction before analysis. Evaluating liquefaction requires knowing the exact time of collection; failure to record collection time prevents determining whether delayed liquefaction (> 60 minutes) is present, which reflects prostatic enzyme deficiency. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 279; PDF p. 304).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Liquefaction of a semen specimen should take place within:
questions.explanation: Normal seminal coagulum undergoes spontaneous liquefaction within 30 to 60 minutes at room temperature through the action of prostatic proteolytic enzymes. Analysis of motility, count, and morphology must wait until liquefaction is complete. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 280; PDF p. 305).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A semen specimen delivered to the laboratory in a condom has a normal sperm count and markedly decreased sperm motility. This indicates:
questions.explanation: Ordinary commercial condoms contain spermicidal chemical lubricants (e.g., nonoxynol-9) and phthalates that immobilize and kill spermatozoa; specimens delivered in ordinary condoms cannot be evaluated for motility or viability and must be rejected. Specialized non-lubricated collection sheaths are required if masturbation is not feasible. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 279; PDF p. 304).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An increased semen pH may be caused by:
questions.explanation: Normal semen pH is slightly alkaline (7.2 to 8.0), reflecting a balance between acidic prostatic secretions and alkaline seminal vesicle fluid. An elevated pH (> 8.0) indicates active infection of the male reproductive tract (e.g., prostatitis) or loss of the acidic first fraction. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 280; PDF p. 305).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Proteolytic enzymes may be added to semen specimens to:
questions.explanation: When a viscous semen specimen fails to liquefy after 1 to 2 hours, physiological pipetting and analysis are impossible. Adding a defined volume of proteolytic enzyme (alpha-chymotrypsin, bromelain, or Dulbecco's buffer) liquefies the specimen, enabling accurate sperm concentration and motility measurements (with appropriate dilution correction). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 280; PDF p. 305).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The normal sperm concentration is:
questions.explanation: The WHO 5th/6th edition criteria define the lower reference limit for normal sperm concentration as 15 x 10^6 sperm/mL (15 million/mL), corresponding to a total sperm count of at least 39 x 10^6 per total ejaculate. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 281; PDF p. 306).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Given the following information, calculate the sperm concentration: dilution, 1:20; sperm counted in five RBC squares on each side of the hemocytometer, 80 and 86; volume, 3 mL.
questions.explanation: Using a 1:20 dilution and counting the 5 small RBC squares in the central large square (volume = 0.02 uL): Concentration = (Count x 20 x 50,000) = Count x 1,000,000 sperm/mL. For 60 sperm counted across the 5 squares, the concentration is 60 x 10^6 sperm/mL (60 million/mL). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 281; PDF p. 306).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Using the information from question 11, calculate the sperm concentration when 80 sperm are counted in 1 WBC square and 86 sperm are counted in another WBC square.
questions.explanation: Total sperm count per ejaculate is obtained by multiplying the sperm concentration (sperm/mL) by the total measured specimen volume (mL). With a concentration of 60 x 10^6 sperm/mL and a volume of 3.0 mL, the total sperm count is 180 million (180 x 10^6). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 281; PDF p. 306).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The primary reason to dilute a semen specimen before performing a sperm concentration is to:
questions.explanation: Semen is diluted with sodium bicarbonate/formalin or saline to completely immobilize rapidly swimming spermatozoa; non-motile sperm can then be visualized and enumerated without double-counting moving cells across grid boundaries. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 281; PDF p. 306).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: When performing a sperm concentration, 60 sperm are counted in the RBC squares on one side of the hemocytometer and 90 sperm are counted in the RBC squares on the other side. The specimen is diluted 1:20. The:
choices: Specimen should be rediluted and counted
Sperm count is greater than 5 million/mL
questions.officialAnswer: Specimen should be rediluted and counted
questions.explanation: Standard quality control requires counting both sides of the hemocytometer; the two counts must agree within 10% (or 5%–10% depending on cell count). If difference exceeds established limits, the dilution is remixed and the hemocytometer reloaded. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 281; PDF p. 306).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Sperm motility evaluations are performed:
choices: Immediately after the specimen is collected
questions.explanation: Motility assessments must be performed on fresh, thoroughly mixed, undiluted semen as soon as liquefaction occurs (within 1 hour of collection), examining a standardized drop under a coverslip at 37°C or room temperature under 40x magnification. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 282; PDF p. 307).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The percentage of sperm showing average motility that is considered normal is:
questions.explanation: Under WHO guidelines, a normal fertile semen sample must have >= 40% total motile spermatozoa (progressive plus non-progressive motility) or >= 32% showing rapid, linear progressive motility within 60 minutes of collection. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 282; PDF p. 307).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The purpose of the acrosomal cap is to:
questions.explanation: The acrosomal cap covers the anterior two-thirds of the sperm head and contains specialized proteolytic enzymes (including hyaluronidase and acrosin) that are released during the acrosome reaction to digest the outer vestments of the ovum (corona radiata and zona pellucida). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 283; PDF p. 308).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The sperm part containing a mitochondrial sheath is the:
questions.explanation: The midpiece (middle piece) of the spermatozoon connects the head to the tail and is surrounded by a dense spiral mitochondrial sheath; these mitochondria oxidize fructose to generate the ATP required to power the axonemal flagellum for propulsion. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 283; PDF p. 308).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are associated with sperm motility except the:
questions.explanation: Flagellar propulsion is driven by dynein ATPase arms in the 9+2 axoneme of the tail powered by midpiece mitochondria. The acrosomal cap contains enzymes for ovum penetration and plays no role in motility. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 283; PDF p. 308).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The morphological shape of a normal sperm head is:
questions.explanation: Under normal morphology criteria, the sperm head must possess an oval, symmetric contour with a clearly demarcated acrosomal region covering 40% to 70% of the head area, free of vacuoles or tapering deformities. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 284; PDF p. 309).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Normal sperm morphology when using the WHO criteria is:
questions.explanation: Under the WHO 5th/6th edition guidelines utilizing Kruger strict morphology scoring, a sample is classified as normal if >= 4% of spermatozoa exhibit strictly normal head, neck, midpiece, and tail dimensions. Under older relaxed traditional WHO criteria, the threshold was >= 30%. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 284; PDF p. 309).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Additional parameters measured by Kruger’s strict morphology include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Kruger strict morphology criteria require precise micrometer measurements: evaluating head size (length 4.0–5.0 um, width 2.5–3.5 um), acrosome area (40%–70%), absence of neck/midpiece angulation (> 90°), and exclusion of all borderline or slightly abnormal forms as defective. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 284; PDF p. 309).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Round cells that are of concern and may be included in sperm counts and morphology analysis are:
questions.explanation: 'Round cells' observed on unstained semen wet mounts comprise two distinct populations: immature germ cells shed from seminiferous epithelium (spermatids/spermatocytes) and white blood cells (leukocytes). Differentiating them via peroxidase staining is essential because > 1 x 10^6 WBCs/mL (leukocytospermia) indicates infection. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 285; PDF p. 310).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: If 5 round cells per 100 sperm are counted in a sperm morphology smear and the sperm concentration is 30 million, the concentration of round cells is:
questions.explanation: Round cell concentration formula: C = (N x S) / 100. If 5 round cells per 100 sperm are observed and the sperm concentration is 60 million/mL: C = (5 x 60) / 100 = 300 / 100 = 3.0 million round cells/mL (3.0 x 10^6/mL). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 285; PDF p. 310).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: After an abnormal sperm motility test with a normal sperm count, what additional test might be ordered?
questions.explanation: When motility is low but concentration is normal, an eosin-nigrosin dye exclusion viability test (or hypo-osmotic swelling test) is performed to differentiate non-viable dead sperm (which take up eosin and stain pink/red due to non-intact membranes) from viable living immotile sperm (which exclude dye and remain unstained bluish-white). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 285; PDF p. 310).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Follow-up testing for a low sperm concentration would include testing for:
questions.explanation: In azoospermic specimens (absence of sperm), seminal fructose testing (using resorcinol) is the essential follow-up assay. Absence of fructose accompanied by low volume (< 1.0 mL) and failure to coagulate indicates congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD) or complete ejaculatory duct obstruction. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 286; PDF p. 311).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The immunobead test for antisperm antibodies:
choices: Detects the presence of male antibodies
Determines the presence of IgG, IgM, and IgA antibodies
Determines the location of antisperm antibodies
questions.explanation: The immunobead assay uses microscopic polyacrylamide spheres coated with anti-human immunoglobulin (IgG, IgA, or IgM). It detects both the class of antisperm antibody present and pinpoints the precise anatomical domain of binding (head, midpiece, main tail piece, or tip). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 286; PDF p. 311).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Measurement of α-glucosidase is performed to detect a disorder of the:
questions.explanation: Neutral alpha-glucosidase is synthesized and secreted exclusively by the epididymal epithelium. Decreased levels in seminal plasma indicate epididymal obstruction or pathology. Prostatic function is assessed by zinc, citric acid, and acid phosphatase; seminal vesicles by fructose. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 287; PDF p. 312).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A specimen delivered to the laboratory with a request for prostatic acid phosphatase and glycoprotein p30 was collected to determine:
questions.explanation: Seminal fluid fructose is produced specifically by the seminal vesicles and serves as the primary metabolic carbohydrate for sperm motility; its measurement is used to assess seminal vesicle secretory function and ductal patency. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 287; PDF p. 312).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: After a negative postvasectomy wet preparation, the specimen should be:
questions.explanation: The prostate gland secretes high concentrations of zinc, citric acid, and prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP); decreased seminal levels of these three markers indicate impaired prostatic secretory function or chronic prostatitis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 287; PDF p. 312).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Standardization of procedures and reference values for semen analysis is provided primarily by the:
questions.explanation: Post-vasectomy evaluations are initiated approximately 2 to 3 months (and after at least 20 ejaculations) following surgery. The specimen is centrifuged and the sediment thoroughly scanned under high power; successful vasectomy requires documenting zero spermatozoa (complete azoospermia) on two consecutive monthly specimens. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 288; PDF p. 313).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The functions of synovial fluid include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Synovial fluid serves three primary mechanical and nutritional functions in diarthrodial joints: (1) providing lubrication to reduce friction between moving joint surfaces, (2) distributing nutrients to the avascular articular cartilage, and (3) absorbing and cushioning shock during mechanical impact or compression. It does not function to remove cartilage debris. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 296; PDF p. 321).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The primary function of synoviocytes is to:
questions.explanation: Synovial fluid is an ultrafiltrate of plasma across the synovial membrane combined with high-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid secreted by specialized synoviocytes. This hyaluronic acid imparts the hallmark high viscosity necessary for joint lubrication. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 296; PDF p. 321).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following tests is not performed frequently on synovial fluid?
questions.explanation: Routine laboratory examination of synovial fluid consists of visual clarity/viscosity assessment, total leukocyte (WBC) count, differential count, crystal identification under polarizing microscopy, Gram stain, and microbiologic culture. Serum uric acid is evaluated first to detect hyperuricemia; direct synovial uric acid measurement is rarely necessary because identifying monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid is definitive for gout. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 296, 301; PDF p. 321, 326).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The procedure for collecting synovial fluid is called:
questions.explanation: The percutaneous needle aspiration of fluid from a joint space is termed arthrocentesis. (Arteriocentesis is arterial puncture, synovialcentesis is nonstandard terminology). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 296; PDF p. 321).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt:
Match the following disorders with their appropriate group:

Categories:
A. Noninflammatory
B. Inflammatory
C. Septic
D. Hemorrhagic

Disorders:
1. Gout
2. Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection
3. Systemic lupus erythematosus
4. Osteoarthritis
5. Hemophilia
6. Rheumatoid arthritis
7. Heparin overdose
questions.officialAnswer: B, C, B, A, D, B, D
questions.explanation: Joint disorders are categorized into four diagnostic pathophysiologic groups based on synovial fluid laboratory findings: Group I Noninflammatory (degenerative joint disease / osteoarthritis); Group II Inflammatory (crystal-induced arthritis such as gout, autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus); Group III Septic (microbial infections, e.g., Neisseria gonorrhoeae); Group IV Hemorrhagic (traumatic injury, hemophilia, anticoagulant therapy/heparin overdose). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 297, Table 12-1; PDF p. 322).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Normal synovial fluid resembles:
questions.explanation: Normal synovial fluid appears clear and pale yellow with high viscosity, closely resembling uncooked egg white; indeed, the term 'synovia' originates from the Latin ovum (egg). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 297; PDF p. 322).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Before testing, very viscous synovial fluid should be treated with:
questions.explanation: High viscosity due to hyaluronic acid impedes accurate pipetting, cell suspension, and chamber loading. Pretreatment with the enzyme hyaluronidase digests hyaluronic acid, reducing viscosity without lysing leukocytes or altering cellular morphology. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 297; PDF p. 322).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The color of the synovial fluid from a patient with a bacterial infection may be:
questions.explanation: In septic arthritis, marked leukocytosis, cellular autolysis, and bacterial metabolites often give the joint fluid a cloudy, purulent appearance with a distinct greenish tinge. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 297; PDF p. 322).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following could be affected most significantly if a synovial fluid is refrigerated before testing?
questions.explanation: Synovial fluid for crystal analysis must be maintained at room temperature and evaluated promptly. Refrigeration decreases solute solubility and can induce artifactual in vitro crystallization of monosodium urate or calcium pyrophosphate, yielding false-positive crystal findings. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 298; PDF p. 323).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The highest WBC count can be expected to be seen in patients with:
questions.explanation: The highest synovial leukocyte counts occur in septic arthritis (Group III), where total WBC counts frequently exceed 50,000 to 100,000/uL (and may reach 200,000/uL) with marked predominance (> 75%) of neutrophils responding to viable bacteria. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 297, Table 12-1; PDF p. 322).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: When diluting a synovial fluid WBC count, all of the following are acceptable except:
questions.explanation: Traditional manual WBC counting diluents containing acetic acid (such as Turk's solution) cannot be used for synovial fluid because acetic acid immediately precipitates hyaluronic acid, forming a firm mucin clot that traps leukocytes and produces falsely low, irregular counts. Isotonic saline, hypotonic saline (which lyses RBCs), or saline with saponin are recommended alternatives. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 297; PDF p. 322).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The lowest percentage of neutrophils would be seen in patients with:
questions.explanation: Noninflammatory joint conditions (such as osteoarthritis) show minimal leukocyte infiltration, with total WBC counts < 1000 to 2000/uL and a low neutrophil differential (< 30%). In contrast, inflammatory conditions have > 50% neutrophils, and septic conditions exceed 75% neutrophils. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 297, Table 12-1; PDF p. 322).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are abnormal when seen in synovial fluid except:
questions.explanation: Primary cellular constituents of normal synovial fluid are mononuclear cells: monocytes, macrophages, and synoviocytes (synovial lining cells). Ragocytes (neutrophils with dark cytoplasmic rheumatoid factor granules), neutrophages, LE cells, and Reiter cells are pathological findings associated with immune complex disease or reactive arthritis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 298; PDF p. 323).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Synovial fluid crystals that occur as a result of purine metabolism or chemotherapy for leukemia are:
questions.explanation: Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals precipitate in joint fluid when uric acid exceeds solubility limits, as in primary gout or secondary hyperuricemia resulting from cytotoxic chemotherapy for leukemia (where accelerated cell lysis releases massive quantities of purine nucleic acids). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 298; PDF p. 323).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Synovial fluid crystals associated with inflammation in patients on dialysis are:
questions.explanation: Calcium oxalate crystals (bipyramidal envelope or square forms) can deposit in synovial fluid and periarticular tissues of patients undergoing long-term renal hemodialysis, producing acute inflammatory arthritis secondary to systemic oxalosis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 298, Table 12-2; PDF p. 323).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Crystals associated with pseudogout are:
questions.explanation: Pseudogout (chondrocalcinosis) is characterized by the intra-articular deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals, typically presenting as rhomboid-shaped or rod-like crystals within synoviocytes and neutrophils. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 298; PDF p. 323).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Synovial fluid for crystal examination should be examined as a/an:
questions.explanation: Synovial fluid crystal evaluation should always be performed initially on an unstained, fresh wet preparation under polarizing and compensated polarizing microscopy. Staining reagents (such as Wright's or Gram stains) contain alcohols and dyes that can dissolve crystals or produce confusing birefringent precipitation artifacts. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 298; PDF p. 323).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Crystals that have the ability to polarize light are:
questions.explanation: All listed crystal types—monosodium urate (MSU), calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD), calcium oxalate, and intra-articular corticosteroid esters—possess anisotropic optical structures that polarize light and produce birefringence. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 298, 300; PDF p. 323, 325).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: In an examination of synovial fluid under compensated polarized light, rhomboid-shaped crystals are observed. What color would these crystals be when aligned parallel to the slow vibration?
questions.explanation: Rhomboid-shaped crystals in synovial fluid represent calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD). Under compensated polarized light, CPPD exhibits positive birefringence. Note on official answer key: The textbook answer key records 'B' (Yellow). In textbook narrative (p. 299, PDF p. 324), CPPD aligned with the slow axis produces a blue color (positive birefringence) and turns yellow when perpendicular. The official answer 'B' is preserved in accordance with the official key, with this optical convention documented. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 299; PDF p. 324).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: If crystals shaped like needles are aligned perpendicular to the slow vibration of compensated polarized light, what color are they?
questions.explanation: Needle-shaped monosodium urate (MSU) crystals possess negative birefringence. When aligned parallel to the slow vibration axis of the first-order red compensator, they appear yellow; when aligned perpendicular to the slow axis, the subtractive retardation reverses to additive retardation, causing the crystal to turn bright blue. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 299; PDF p. 324).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Negative birefringence occurs under red-compensated polarized light when:
choices: Slow light is impeded more than fast light
Slow light is impeded less than fast light
Fast light runs against the molecular grain of the crystal
questions.officialAnswer: Fast light runs against the molecular grain of the crystal
questions.explanation: Negative birefringence in MSU crystals occurs because the crystal's molecular lattice runs parallel to its longitudinal axis. When the crystal is aligned with the compensator's slow axis, the fast ray of polarized light travels perpendicular across the molecular grain, experiencing maximum impedance (subtraction of velocity from the fast ray), which produces yellow light. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 299; PDF p. 324).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Often synovial fluid cultures are plated on chocolate agar to detect the presence of:
questions.explanation: Synovial fluid is routinely inoculated onto chocolate agar in addition to blood agar and thioglycollate broth because Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a fastidious pathogen that requires enriched chocolate agar and carbon dioxide, and is the predominant cause of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 301; PDF p. 326).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The chemical test performed most frequently on synovial fluid is:
questions.explanation: Glucose is the most commonly requested and clinically informative chemistry test on synovial fluid. Markedly decreased synovial fluid glucose (normally within 10 mg/dL of simultaneous fasting serum glucose) is a hallmark of inflammatory (Group II) and septic (Group III) joint disorders resulting from leukocyte and bacterial glycolysis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 301; PDF p. 326).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following chemistry tests can be performed on synovial fluid to determine the severity of RA?
questions.explanation: Synovial fluid lysosomal enzymes—including acid phosphatase, alkaline phosphatase, and lactate dehydrogenase (LD)—are released by proliferating synovial lining cells and infiltrating leukocytes during rheumatoid synovitis; their activity correlates directly with local tissue destruction and the severity and prognosis of rheumatoid arthritis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 301; PDF p. 326).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Serological tests on patients’ serum may be performed to detect antibodies causing arthritis for all of the following disorders except:
questions.explanation: Serological testing detects systemic antibodies responsible for autoimmune arthropathies (rheumatoid factor in RA, ANA in systemic lupus erythematosus) or infectious arthropathies (Lyme disease serology). Pseudogout is a metabolic and degenerative crystal deposition disease (calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate) that has no antibody etiology and cannot be diagnosed by serological antibody testing. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 12, Book p. 301; PDF p. 326).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of serous fluid is to:
questions.explanation: Serous fluid is an ultrafiltrate of plasma present in small volumes within the closed pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal cavities. Its primary physiological function is to provide lubrication between the parietal and visceral serous membranes, minimizing friction and mechanical irritation during continuous organ motion. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 306; PDF p. 331).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The membrane that lines the wall of a cavity is the:
questions.explanation: Serous cavities are lined by two contiguous mesothelial membranes: the parietal membrane, which directly lines the interior cavity wall, and the visceral membrane, which closely covers the external surface of the enclosed organs. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 306; PDF p. 331).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: During normal production of serous fluid, the slight excess of fluid is:
questions.explanation: Serous fluid forms as an ultrafiltrate across parietal capillary walls; the small volume of physiological excess fluid is continually drained and reabsorbed by parietal lymphatic capillaries, maintaining a constant dynamic balance and preventing cavity distension. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 306; PDF p. 331).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Production of serous fluid is controlled by:
questions.explanation: According to Starling's law of the capillary, serous fluid dynamics depend on the interplay of capillary hydrostatic pressure (forcing fluid out), colloidal oncotic pressure (drawing fluid in), and capillary endothelial permeability. Alterations in any of these parameters can disrupt equilibrium and induce effusion formation. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 306; PDF p. 331).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An increase in the amount of serous fluid is called a/an:
questions.explanation: An abnormal pathological accumulation of fluid within a serous cavity resulting from disrupted filtration, reabsorption, or lymphatic drainage is designated an effusion. (Transudates and exudates are specific subtypes of effusions). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 306; PDF p. 331).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Pleural fluid is collected by:
questions.explanation: The clinical procedure for collecting pleural fluid via percutaneous needle puncture through the chest wall into the pleural space is thoracentesis. (Paracentesis refers to peritoneal aspiration; pericardiocentesis refers to pericardial aspiration). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 307; PDF p. 332).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt:
Place the appropriate letter in front of the following statements describing transudates and exudates:

Categories:
A. Transudate
B. Exudate

Statements:
1. Caused by increased hydrostatic pressure
2. Caused by increased capillary permeability
3. Caused by decreased oncotic pressure
4. Caused by congestive heart failure
5. Malignancy related
6. Tuberculosis related
7. Endocarditis related
8. Clear appearance
questions.officialAnswer: B, A, A, A, B, B, B, A
questions.explanation: Transudates (A) arise from systemic non-inflammatory imbalances in hydrostatic pressure (e.g., congestive heart failure) or oncotic pressure (e.g., hypoproteinemia) and present with a clear appearance. Exudates (B) result from direct inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic damage to serous membranes (increased capillary permeability, tuberculosis, endocarditis, malignancy). Note on official answer key: The textbook answer key records 'B, A, A, A, B, B, B, A', transposing the first two statements (increased hydrostatic pressure is transudative [A] and increased capillary permeability is exudative [B]). Official answer is preserved and discrepancy documented. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 307, Table 13-1; PDF p. 332).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Fluid: serum protein and lactic dehydrogenase ratios are performed on serous fluids:
choices: To determine the type of serous fluid
When a traumatic tap has occurred
questions.explanation: According to Light's criteria, calculating the pleural fluid-to-serum protein ratio (exudate if > 0.5) and fluid-to-serum lactic dehydrogenase (LD) ratio (exudate if > 0.6, or fluid LD > 2/3 upper limit of normal serum LD) provides the standard, highly sensitive laboratory method to classify an effusion as a transudate or an exudate. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 307; PDF p. 332).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following requires the most additional testing?
questions.explanation: Transudates reflect underlying systemic hemodynamic conditions (such as CHF) and generally require no further fluid evaluation. In contrast, exudates require extensive workup—including cell differential, microbiological culture and stains, tumor markers, and cytopathology—to uncover localized infectious, inflammatory, or malignant etiologies. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 307; PDF p. 332).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An additional test performed on pleural fluid to classify the fluid as a transudate or exudate is the:
questions.explanation: Pleural fluid cholesterol concentration (> 60 mg/dL) and fluid-to-serum cholesterol ratio (> 0.3) provide highly accurate auxiliary markers to distinguish exudates from transudates, particularly in borderline effusions or when diuresis alters protein ratios. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 308; PDF p. 333).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A milky-appearing pleural fluid indicates:
questions.explanation: A milky appearance in pleural fluid occurs in two distinct clinical conditions: chylous effusions, caused by thoracic duct obstruction or trauma/leakage (rich in triglycerides and chylomicrons), and pseudochylous effusions, caused by chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid pleuritis or tuberculosis (rich in cholesterol crystals and cellular breakdown products). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 308; PDF p. 333).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following best represents a hemothorax?
questions.explanation: A hemothorax is diagnostically defined when the pleural fluid hematocrit exceeds 50% of the patient's peripheral blood hematocrit. With a blood hematocrit of 30%, a fluid hematocrit of 20% (66.7% of blood HCT) confirms a true hemothorax rather than a hemorrhagic effusion or traumatic tap. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 308; PDF p. 333).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are normal cells seen in pleural fluid except:
questions.explanation: Normal cellular elements in serous cavities consist of benign mesothelial lining cells, macrophages, small resting lymphocytes, and rare neutrophils. Mesothelioma cells are neoplastic cells derived from primary pleural malignancy (malignant mesothelioma, often asbestos-related) and are never normal. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 309; PDF p. 334).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A differential observation of pleural fluid associated with tuberculosis is:
questions.explanation: Tuberculous pleurisy induces intense lymphocytic exudation with a thick fibrinous coating over the pleural lining, preventing mesothelial desquamation; hence, the microscopic hallmark of tuberculous effusions is high lymphocyte counts accompanied by a marked absence (< 1%) of mesothelial cells. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 309; PDF p. 334).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are characteristics of malignant cells except:
questions.explanation: Cytological hallmarks of malignancy include prominent multiple nucleoli, cellular and nuclear pleomorphism, nuclear hyperchromasia, cell cannibalism, cytoplasmic molding, and high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratios. Absence of nucleoli is a feature of quiescent benign cells, not malignant cells. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 310; PDF p. 335).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A pleural fluid pH of 6.0 indicates:
questions.explanation: A pleural fluid pH dropping down to ~6.0 or below is a clinical medical emergency that specifically indicates esophageal perforation or rupture, as gastric hydrochloric acid leaks directly into the mediastinum and pleural space. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 311; PDF p. 336).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Plasma cells seen in pleural fluid indicate:
questions.explanation: Plasma cells in pleural fluid signify a chronic cell-mediated and humoral immune response, most commonly encountered alongside marked lymphocytosis in chronic tuberculous pleurisy. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 309; PDF p. 334).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A significant cell found in pericardial or pleural fluid that should be referred to cytology is a:
questions.explanation: Mesothelioma cells represent an aggressive primary pleural or pericardial malignancy; any clusters of atypical, pleomorphic, or multi-nucleated mesothelial cells must be immediately documented and submitted for formal cytopathologic and immunohistochemical evaluation. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 310; PDF p. 335).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Another name for a peritoneal effusion is:
questions.explanation: An abnormal accumulation of serous effusion within the peritoneal cavity is clinically and historically referred to as ascites, and the aspirated specimen is designated ascitic fluid. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 314; PDF p. 339).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A test performed primarily on peritoneal lavage fluid is a/an:
questions.explanation: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) is utilized in acute trauma settings to assess blunt abdominal injury; the primary test performed is the erythrocyte (RBC) count, where values > 100,000/uL confirm significant internal hemoperitoneum requiring surgical exploration. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 314; PDF p. 339).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The recommended test for determining whether peritoneal fluid is a transudate or an exudate is the:
questions.explanation: The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG), calculated as Serum Albumin - Ascitic Fluid Albumin, has superseded traditional protein and LD ratios for peritoneal fluid. A difference >= 1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension (transudate), whereas a difference < 1.1 g/dL indicates exudative etiology without portal hypertension. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 314; PDF p. 339).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Given the following results, classify this peritoneal fluid: serum albumin, 2.2 g/dL; serum protein, 6.0 g/dL; fluid albumin, 1.6 g/dL.
questions.explanation: Given serum albumin = 2.2 g/dL and fluid albumin = 1.6 g/dL: SAAG = 2.2 - 1.6 = 0.6 g/dL. Because the gradient (0.6) is less than 1.1 g/dL, the peritoneal fluid is classified as an exudate (peritoneal inflammation, infection, or malignancy). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 314; PDF p. 339).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Differentiation between bacterial peritonitis and cirrhosis is done by performing a/an:
questions.explanation: To distinguish spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) from uncomplicated ascitic transudates in cirrhotic patients, an absolute neutrophil count (ANC = Total WBC x % neutrophils) is calculated; an ANC > 250 cells/uL indicates active bacterial infection. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 315; PDF p. 340).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Detection of the CA 125 tumor marker in peritoneal fluid indicates:
questions.explanation: Elevated cancer antigen 125 (CA 125) in peritoneal fluid strongly correlates with ovarian carcinoma or other female reproductive tract malignancies, distinguishing them from gastrointestinal cancers (which typically elevate CEA). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 316; PDF p. 341).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Chemical tests primarily performed on peritoneal fluid include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Standard chemical assays performed on peritoneal fluid include glucose (decreased in peritonitis/malignancy), amylase (pancreatitis or bowel perforation), alkaline phosphatase (intestinal perforation), and BUN/creatinine (bladder rupture). Calcium is not a routine diagnostic analyte for peritoneal fluid. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 315; PDF p. 340).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Cultures of peritoneal fluid are incubated:
questions.explanation: Peritoneal infections, particularly secondary to gastrointestinal tract perforation or pelvic infection, frequently involve polymicrobial flora comprising both facultative and strict anaerobic organisms (e.g., Bacteroides fragilis). Therefore, cultures must be incubated both aerobically and anaerobically. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 316; PDF p. 341).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following could be diagnosed by collecting and analyzing a BAL except:
questions.explanation: Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is designed specifically to sample cellular, biochemical, and microbiological components of the lower respiratory tract (alveoli and terminal bronchioles). It is diagnostic for interstitial lung disease, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, environmental pneumoconioses (asbestosis, silicosis), and opportunistic pneumonias. Meningitis affects the meninges and subarachnoid space and is evaluated exclusively by lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 320; PDF p. 345).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: What procedure is used for bronchoalveolar lavage?
questions.explanation: BAL fluid is obtained by inserting a flexible fiberoptic bronchoscope through the trachea and into a segmental or subsegmental bronchus of the selected lung lobe until it is wedged. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 320; PDF p. 345).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: In bronchoalveolar lavage, the targeted area of the lung is:
questions.explanation: The wedged alveolar subsegment is repeatedly instilled with aliquots of warm, sterile, nonbacteriostatic isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl), which washes out cells and secretions before immediate gentle syringe or wall aspiration. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 320; PDF p. 345).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A BAL fluid that appears orange-red is an indication of which of the following:
choices: Patient who is a heavy smoker
questions.explanation: Fresh, acute intra-alveolar hemorrhage yields increasingly bloody, bright red aliquots. In contrast, an older alveolar hemorrhage syndrome displays an orange-red to golden-brown fluid coloration due to in vivo erythrocyte breakdown and macrophage conversion of hemoglobin to hemosiderin and bilirubin/hematoidin pigments. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 321; PDF p. 346).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Cell counts from a BAL fluid must be performed within:
questions.explanation: Because alveolar macrophages and neutrophils in BAL fluid undergo rapid in vitro degeneration, autolysis, and clumping, total and differential cell counts must be performed within 1 hour of collection (or the specimen placed on ice). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 321; PDF p. 346).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: An elevated CD4/CD8 lymphocyte ratio indicates:
questions.explanation: In pulmonary sarcoidosis, activated CD4+ helper T-lymphocytes selectively accumulate in the lung parenchyma and alveoli, markedly elevating the CD4:CD8 ratio (often > 3.5:1 to 4.0:1), compared to normal ratios (~1.5:1) or decreased ratios seen in hypersensitivity pneumonitis and HIV. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 322; PDF p. 347).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Immunological study of cells is typically performed by:
questions.explanation: Quantitative identification of lymphocyte subpopulations (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19, CD56) and cell surface antigen markers is performed by multiparameter flow cytometry using fluorochrome-conjugated monoclonal antibodies. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 322; PDF p. 347).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The cell in a BAL fluid seen most frequently is:
questions.explanation: In healthy, nonsmoking individuals, alveolar macrophages constitute the vast majority of cells recovered in BAL fluid, normally accounting for 80% to 90% of total leukocytes. Lymphocytes represent 5% to 15%, neutrophils < 3%, and eosinophils < 1%. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 321, Table 14-1; PDF p. 346).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: What is an opportunistic pathogen in patients with AIDS that can be recovered in BAL fluid?
questions.explanation: Patients with advanced HIV infection/AIDS frequently develop life-threatening opportunistic fungal pneumonias; Cryptococcus neoformans (demonstrated by encapsulated budding yeast with India ink, mucicarmine, or cryptococcal antigen) and Pneumocystis jirovecii are classic opportunistic agents isolated from BAL specimens. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 323; PDF p. 348).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The stain used in cytology for the diagnosis of lipid-laden alveolar macrophages is:
questions.explanation: Lipid-laden alveolar macrophages (LLAMs, indicative of aspiration syndromes or pulmonary alveolar proteinosis) are cytologically confirmed by staining with neutral lipid stains such as Sudan III or Oil Red O, which color intracellular neutral lipid droplets bright orange-red. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 14, Book p. 323; PDF p. 348).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a function of amniotic fluid?
choices: Allows exchange of carbon dioxide and oxygen
Protects the fetus from extreme temperature changes
Acts as a protective cushion for the fetus
questions.officialAnswer: Allows exchange of carbon dioxide and oxygen
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid performs vital mechanical, thermal, and developmental protective functions: cushioning the fetus against external maternal abdominal trauma, permitting free fetal musculoskeletal movement, maintaining stable thermal equilibrium, and facilitating symmetrical lung growth. Respiratory gas exchange (oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide elimination) is mediated by the umbilical-placental circulation, not by amniotic fluid. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 328; PDF p. 353).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: What is the primary cause of the normal increase in amniotic fluid as a pregnancy progresses?
choices: Transfer of water across the placenta
questions.explanation: While initial first-trimester amniotic fluid is an ultrafiltrate of maternal plasma, after approximately 16 weeks' gestation fetal micturition (fetal urine production) becomes the primary source contributing to the progressive volume expansion of amniotic fluid. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 328; PDF p. 353).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a reason for decreased amounts of amniotic fluid?
questions.explanation: Oligohydramnios (decreased volume) results from conditions that decrease fluid entry (fetal urinary tract obstruction, renal agenesis) or increase fluid loss (premature rupture of membranes, excessive fetal swallowing). Fetal failure to swallow (e.g., due to anencephaly or esophageal atresia) prevents normal reabsorption and results in polyhydramnios (excessive fluid), not oligohydramnios. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 328; PDF p. 353).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Why might a creatinine level be requested on an amniotic fluid?
choices: Differentiate amniotic fluid from maternal urine
questions.officialAnswer: Differentiate amniotic fluid from maternal urine
questions.explanation: Accidental puncture of the maternal bladder during amniocentesis produces a fluid specimen that can mimic amniotic fluid. Because urine contains high concentrations of metabolic waste products, measuring creatinine (> 10 mg/dL in urine vs. <= 3.5 mg/dL in amniotic fluid) and urea nitrogen differentiates maternal urine from genuine amniotic fluid. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 329; PDF p. 354).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Amniotic fluid specimens are placed in amber-colored tubes before sending them to the laboratory to prevent the destruction of:
questions.explanation: Bilirubin is extremely photo-labile; exposure to ambient room light or sunlight causes rapid photochemical oxidation of unconjugated bilirubin to biliverdin, which falsely flattens the 450-nm spectrophotometric absorbance peak and underestimates the severity of fetal hemolysis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 330; PDF p. 355).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: How are specimens for FLM testing delivered to and stored in the laboratory?
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid specimens submitted for fetal lung maturity (FLM) phospholipid evaluation (L/S ratio, PG, lamellar body count) must be transported on wet ice and refrigerated upon receipt to prevent enzymatic degradation and chemical deterioration of surfactant phospholipids by endogenous amniotic lipases. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 330; PDF p. 355).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Why are amniotic specimens for cytogenetic analysis incubated at 37°C before analysis?
choices: To detect the presence of meconium
To differentiate amniotic fluid from urine
To prevent photo-oxidation of bilirubin to biliverdin
To prolong fetal cell viability and integrity
questions.officialAnswer: To prolong fetal cell viability and integrity
questions.explanation: Cytogenetic and chromosomal karyotyping studies require viable, mitotically active fetal cells. Specimens must never be frozen or chilled, and maintaining them at 37°C (or controlled room temperature) preserves the viability of desquamated fetal amniocytes required for successful in vitro cell culture growth. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 330; PDF p. 355).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt:
Match the following colors in amniotic fluid with their significance:

Colors:
A. Colorless
B. Dark green
C. Red-brown
D. Yellow

Significance:
1. Fetal death
2. Normal
3. Presence of bilirubin
4. Presence of meconium
questions.explanation: Diagnostic color associations in amniotic fluid: Colorless to pale straw = Normal physiological fluid (2); Dark green = Passage of fetal meconium indicating fetal hypoxia/distress (4); Red-brown = Fetal death and maceration with intra-amniotic hemoglobin breakdown (1); Yellow = Presence of bilirubin from erythroblastosis fetalis / hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (3). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 330; PDF p. 355).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A significant rise in the OD of amniotic fluid at 450 nm indicates the presence of which analyte?
questions.explanation: Unconjugated bilirubin exhibits a distinct optical absorbance maximum at 450 nm. In spectrophotometric fluid analysis, the difference between the baseline curve and the 450-nm peak (Delta A450) quantitatively reflects the concentration of indirect bilirubin produced by fetal erythrocyte destruction. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 331; PDF p. 356).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Plotting the amniotic fluid OD on a Liley graph represents the severity of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. A value that is plotted in zone II indicates what condition of the fetus?
choices: Moderately affected fetus that requires close monitoring
Severely affected fetus that requires intervention
questions.officialAnswer: Moderately affected fetus that requires close monitoring
questions.explanation: On the classic three-zone Liley graph, values plotted within Zone II represent a moderately affected fetus experiencing active isoimmunization hemolysis; such pregnancies require rigorous serial surveillance (amniocentesis or Doppler ultrasound of middle cerebral artery) and may necessitate intrauterine transfusion if the curve ascends toward Zone III. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 331; PDF p. 356).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The presence of a fetal neural tube disorder may be detected by:
questions.explanation: Open neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly) allow fetal cerebrospinal and tissue fluids to leak directly into the amniotic cavity, dramatically increasing amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein (AFAFP) and subsequent maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 332; PDF p. 357).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: True or False: An AFP MoM value greater than two times the median value is considered an indication of a neural tube disorder.
questions.explanation: Maternal serum and amniotic fluid AFP concentrations are expressed as multiples of the median (MoM) to account for gestational age variations; values exceeding 2.0 to 2.5 MoM are statistically abnormal and indicative of open neural tube defects or ventral wall defects (omphalocele/gastroschisis). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 332; PDF p. 357).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: When severe HDFN is present, which of the following tests on the amniotic fluid would the physician not order to determine whether the fetal lungs are mature enough to withstand a premature delivery?
questions.explanation: When considering early delivery of a fetus compromised by severe Rh isoimmunization, the physician assesses surfactant and pulmonary readiness using fetal lung maturity assays (L/S ratio, PG, Foam Stability Index, lamellar body counts). Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) assesses neural tube closure and abdominal wall integrity, having no relationship to alveolar surfactant production. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 333; PDF p. 358).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: True or False: Before 35 weeks’ gestation, the normal L/S ratio is less than 1.6.
questions.explanation: Before approximately 35 weeks' gestation, alveolar type II pneumocytes synthesize lecithin at low levels that parallel sphingomyelin concentration, resulting in an immature L/S ratio consistently below 1.6. After 35 weeks, lecithin production sharply surges, driving the mature ratio to >= 2.0. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 333; PDF p. 358).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: When performing an L/S ratio by thin-layer chromatography, a mature fetal lung will show:
choices: Sphingomyelin twice as concentrated as lecithin
Lecithin twice as concentrated as sphingomyelin
Equal concentrations of lecithin and sphingomyelin
questions.officialAnswer: Lecithin twice as concentrated as sphingomyelin
questions.explanation: In thin-layer chromatography (TLC) evaluation of amniotic phospholipids, pulmonary maturity is achieved when the densitometric concentration of lecithin (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) is at least twice that of sphingomyelin (L/S ratio >= 2.0), indicating sufficient surfactant to prevent neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 333; PDF p. 358).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: True or False: Phosphatidyl glycerol is present with an L/S ratio of 1.1.
questions.explanation: Phosphatidylglycerol (PG) is an independent pulmonary surfactant component. Although PG normally appears around 35 to 36 weeks alongside the lecithin surge, it can be detected in the presence of an L/S ratio < 2.0 (such as 1.1) in pregnancies characterized by chronic intrauterine stress or premature rupture of membranes; when PG is present, neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is exceedingly rare regardless of the L/S ratio. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 334; PDF p. 359).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A rapid immunologic test for FLM that does not require performance of thin-layer chromatography is:
