questions.explanation: The Amniostat-FLM assay provides a rapid, semiquantitative latex agglutination method for detecting phosphatidylglycerol directly in amniotic fluid using specific anti-PG antibodies; it bypasses tedious thin-layer chromatography and is not invalidated by blood or meconium contamination. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 334; PDF p. 359).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Does the failure to produce bubbles in the Foam Stability Index indicate increased or decreased lecithin?
questions.explanation: In the foam stability ('shake') test, surfactant reduces surface tension to produce a persistent meniscus ring of foam despite the presence of ethanol (an antifoaming agent). Failure of the fluid to generate and maintain stable bubbles indicates inadequate surfactant/lecithin concentration, signifying fetal pulmonary immaturity. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 334; PDF p. 359).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The presence of phosphatidyl glycerol in amniotic fluid fetal lung maturity tests must be confirmed when:
choices: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn is present
Amniotic fluid is contaminated by hemoglobin
A neural tube disorder is suspected
questions.explanation: Maternal diabetes mellitus delays fetal type II pneumocyte enzymatic maturation; in diabetic pregnancies, severe respiratory distress syndrome frequently occurs despite an ostensibly mature L/S ratio of 2.0. Therefore, documentation of phosphatidylglycerol (PG) is mandatory before elective delivery in diabetic gravidas. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 334; PDF p. 359).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A lamellar body count of 50,000 correlates with:
choices: Absent phosphatidyl glycerol and L/S ratio of 1.0
L/S ratio of 1.5 and absent phosphatidyl glycerol
OD at 650 nm of 1.010 and an L/S ratio of 1.1
OD at 650 nm of 0.150 and an L/S ratio of 2.0
questions.officialAnswer: OD at 650 nm of 0.150 and an L/S ratio of 2.0
questions.explanation: Lamellar bodies represent the storage and secretory form of pulmonary surfactant. When counted on automated impedance cell counters (using the platelet aperture due to size similarity, 1–5 um), a lamellar body count (LBC) of 50,000/uL correlates directly with an optical density >= 0.150 at 650 nm and an established mature L/S ratio >= 2.0. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 335; PDF p. 360).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: In what part of the digestive tract do pancreatic enzymes and bile salts contribute to digestion?
questions.explanation: Enzymatic breakdown of dietary macromolecules occurs predominantly in the duodenum and jejunum of the small intestine, where pancreatic digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, trypsin, chymotrypsin) and hepatic bile salts emulsify fats and digest carbohydrates and proteins. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 340; PDF p. 365).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Where does the reabsorption of water take place in the primary digestive process?
questions.explanation: The cecum, colon, and rectum of the large intestine are primarily responsible for the efficient reabsorption of water (approximately 90% of the fluid delivered from the ileum) and electrolytes, compacting the fecal mass prior to evacuation. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 340; PDF p. 365).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following tests is not performed to detect osmotic diarrhea?
questions.explanation: Osmotic diarrhea is driven by retention of unabsorbed, osmotically active luminal solutes; diagnostic tests include fecal reducing substances (Clinitest), microscopic muscle fibers (undigested protein), and qualitative/quantitative fecal lipids. Fecal neutrophils are a diagnostic marker for invasive mucosal inflammation (inflammatory diarrhea), not osmotic diarrhea. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 341; PDF p. 366).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The normal composition of feces includes all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Normal stool contains water, commensal enteric microflora (up to one-third of dry weight), desquamated intestinal epithelial cells, electrolytes, and unabsorbed dietary fiber. Blood (erythrocytes/hemoglobin) is never a normal constituent and indicates gastrointestinal hemorrhage, ulceration, or neoplasm. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 340; PDF p. 365).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: What is the fecal test that requires a 3-day specimen?
questions.explanation: Because gastrointestinal transit times and stool evacuation vary widely from day to day, accurate quantitative measurement of fecal lipids (e.g., Van de Kamer titration) requires a strict 72-hour (3-day) timed stool collection while maintaining a standardized 100 g/day dietary fat regimen. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 341; PDF p. 366).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The normal brown color of the feces is produced by:
questions.explanation: Bilirubin excreted into the bile is deconjugated and reduced by colonic bacteria into urobilinogens (stercobilinogen); spontaneous oxidation of these colorless compounds forms urobilin (stercobilin), which gives normal stool its characteristic brown pigmentation. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 341; PDF p. 366).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Diarrhea can result from all of the following except:
choices: Addition of pathogenic organisms to the normal intestinal flora
Disruption of the normal intestinal bacterial flora
Increased reabsorption of intestinal water and electrolytes
questions.officialAnswer: Increased reabsorption of intestinal water and electrolytes
questions.explanation: Diarrhea is characterized by increased stool fluidity and volume resulting from decreased intestinal water absorption or excessive solute secretion. Increased mucosal reabsorption of water dehydrates feces, producing hard, scybalous stools characteristic of constipation. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 340; PDF p. 365).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Stools from people with steatorrhea will contain excess amounts of:
questions.explanation: Steatorrhea refers specifically to the pathological excretion of abnormal quantities of unabsorbed lipids in feces (fecal fat > 7 g/24 h), typical of pancreatic insufficiency or small bowel malabsorptive sprue. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 341; PDF p. 366).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following pairings of stool appearance and cause do not match?
questions.explanation: Radiographic contrast procedures utilizing barium sulfate coat the gastrointestinal lumen and impart a chalky, pale white appearance to evacuated stools. Yellow-green stools reflect unoxidized biliverdin or ingestion of chlorophyll-rich vegetables. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 342, Table 16-1; PDF p. 367).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Stool specimens that appear ribbon-like are indicative of which condition?
questions.explanation: A distinct, persistent pencil-thin or ribbon-like morphology of formed feces reflects mechanical luminal narrowing or extrinsic compression of the distal colon/rectum, most commonly caused by colon carcinoma, strictures, or obstructive polyps. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 342; PDF p. 367).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A black tarry stool is indicative of:
questions.explanation: Melena (black, sticky, tarry feces) indicates substantial bleeding (> 50–100 mL) originating from the upper gastrointestinal tract (esophagus, stomach, duodenum); gastric hydrochloric acid and digestive enzymes degrade hemoglobin into black acid hematin during prolonged transit. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 342; PDF p. 367).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Chemical screening tests performed on feces include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The pilocarpine iontophoresis sweat test measures sweat chloride on the skin to diagnose cystic fibrosis, not on fecal specimens. APT, Clinitest, and fecal fat titrations are performed directly on feces. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 344; PDF p. 369).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Secretory diarrhea is caused by:
questions.explanation: Secretory diarrhea is triggered by enterotoxins (such as cholera toxin produced by Vibrio cholerae) that activate mucosal enterocyte adenylate cyclase, resulting in massive active secretion of chloride and water into the lumen exceeding colonic reabsorptive capacity. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 340; PDF p. 365).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The fecal osmotic gap is elevated in which disorder?
questions.explanation: The fecal osmotic gap is calculated as 290 - 2 x (Fecal Sodium + Fecal Potassium). In osmotic diarrhea, unmeasured, unabsorbed solutes (carbohydrates, magnesium) drive luminal osmolality, creating an elevated gap (> 50 mOsm/kg). In secretory diarrhea, secreted electrolytes account for all osmolality, so the gap is low (< 50 mOsm/kg). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 341; PDF p. 366).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Microscopic examination of stools provides preliminary information as to the cause of diarrhea because:
choices: Neutrophils are present in conditions caused by toxin-producing bacteria
Neutrophils are present in conditions that affect the intestinal wall
Red and white blood cells are present if the cause is bacterial
Neutrophils are present if the condition is of nonbacterial etiology
questions.officialAnswer: Neutrophils are present in conditions that affect the intestinal wall
questions.explanation: Stool microscopy for leukocytes (stained with methylene blue, Wright's, or Gram stain) rapidly separates invasive mucosal pathogens that induce an acute inflammatory response (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, C. difficile) from toxigenic pathogens or viruses that cause secretory/osmotic diarrhea without mucosal invasion. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 342; PDF p. 367).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: True or False: The presence of fecal neutrophils would be expected with diarrhea caused by a rotavirus.
questions.explanation: Rotavirus infects and blunts villous enterocytes without inducing mucosal ulceration or acute suppurative inflammation; consequently, fecal neutrophils are not present in rotavirus gastroenteritis. Official answer: False. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 342; PDF p. 367).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Large orange-red droplets seen on direct microscopic examination of stools mixed with Sudan III represent:
questions.explanation: In qualitative fecal fat microscopy, neutral fats (unhydrolyzed triglycerides) stain directly with Sudan III without requiring chemical pretreatment, appearing as large, bright orange-red refractile globules under low and high power. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 343; PDF p. 368).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Microscopic examination of stools mixed with Sudan III and glacial acetic acid and then heated will show small orange-red droplets that represent:
choices: Fatty acids, soaps, and neutral fats
questions.officialAnswer: Fatty acids, soaps, and neutral fats
questions.explanation: Acetic acid and heat hydrolyze insoluble fatty acid soaps (calcium/magnesium soaps) and split ester bonds; upon gentle boiling and cooling with Sudan III, neutral fats, free fatty acids, and hydrolyzed soaps all coalesce into visible orange-red droplets, representing total fecal lipid content. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 343; PDF p. 368).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: When performing a microscopic stool examination for muscle fibers, the structures that should be counted:
choices: Have vertical striations and stain red
questions.explanation: Diagnostic evaluation of creatorrhea (impaired proteolytic digestion) requires counting undigested meat fibers, which retain well-preserved rectangular shapes and distinct, two-dimensional orthogonal (longitudinal and cross) striations in 10% alcoholic eosin. Partially digested fibers exhibit striations in only one dimension. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 343; PDF p. 368).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A value of 85% fat retention would indicate:
questions.explanation: The coefficient of fat retention is calculated as: [(Dietary Fat - Fecal Fat) / Dietary Fat] x 100. In healthy adults consuming 100 g fat/day, at least 95% of ingested fat is absorbed. A retention coefficient of 85% reflects abnormal lipid loss (15 g fat excreted), confirming steatorrhea. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 344; PDF p. 369).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following tests would not be indicative of steatorrhea?
questions.explanation: Diagnostic workup of steatorrhea focuses on lipid excretion and exocrine pancreatic capacity (Sudan III, quantitative fat, fecal elastase-1). Testing for fecal occult blood screens for mucosal vascular erosion, polyps, or colorectal neoplasia and is not an indicator of lipid malabsorption. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 343; PDF p. 368).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The term “occult” blood describes blood that:
choices: Is produced in the lower GI tract
Is produced in the upper GI tract
Is not visibly apparent in the stool specimen
questions.officialAnswer: Is not visibly apparent in the stool specimen
questions.explanation: Occult blood refers to microscopic or concealed gastrointestinal bleeding (< 2.5 mL/day) that does not alter the macroscopic color or consistency of the stool, necessitating chemical or immunochemical screening methods for detection. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 344; PDF p. 369).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: What is the recommended number of specimens that should be tested to confirm a negative occult blood result?
choices: Two samples taken from different parts of three stool specimens
Three samples taken from the outermost portion of the stool specimen
Three samples taken from different parts of two stool specimens
questions.officialAnswer: Two samples taken from different parts of three stool specimens
questions.explanation: Because neoplastic lesions, adenomatous polyps, and ulcers bleed intermittently and blood is distributed non-homogeneously throughout the fecal bolus, standard guaiac screening protocols require sampling two distinct areas from each of three consecutively passed stool specimens (six total test windows). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 345; PDF p. 370).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The immunochemical tests for occult blood:
choices: Give false-positive reactions with meat hemoglobin
Can give false-positive reactions with aspirin
questions.explanation: Fecal immunochemical tests (FIT/iFOBT) employ specific antibodies directed against the globin moiety of human hemoglobin. Because globin from upper GI bleeding is digested by duodenal proteases and animal myoglobin does not cross-react, FIT is highly specific for lower GI bleeding and requires no dietary restrictions. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 345; PDF p. 370).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Guaiac tests for detecting occult blood rely on the:
choices: Reaction of hemoglobin with hydrogen peroxide
questions.explanation: The traditional chemical fecal occult blood test (gFOBT) exploits the pseudoperoxidase catalytic activity of the heme prosthetic group, which catalyzes the transfer of oxygen from hydrogen peroxide developer to phenolic guaiac resin, producing a characteristic quinone blue chromogen. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 344; PDF p. 369).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: What is the significance of an APT test that remains pink after the addition of sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: The Apt-Downey test determines whether bloody stool/emesis from a neonate represents swallowed maternal blood from delivery or active neonatal gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Fetal hemoglobin (Hb F) resists alkaline denaturation by 1% NaOH and maintains a distinct pink solution, whereas adult hemoglobin (Hb A) rapidly denatures into yellow-brown alkaline hematin within 1 to 2 minutes. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 346; PDF p. 371).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: In the Van de Kamer method for quantitative fecal fat determinations, fecal lipids are:
choices: Converted to fatty acids before titrating with sodium hydroxide
Homogenized and titrated to a neutral endpoint with sodium hydroxide
Measured by spectrophotometer after addition of Sudan III
questions.officialAnswer: Converted to fatty acids before titrating with sodium hydroxide
questions.explanation: The Van de Kamer quantitative fecal fat titration method involves alkaline saponification of neutral fats and soaps, acid cleavage with HCl to liberate free fatty acids, organic solvent extraction, and subsequent neutralization titration of the extracted fatty acids against standardized sodium hydroxide (NaOH). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 344; PDF p. 369).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A patient whose stool exhibits increased fats, undigested muscle fibers, and the inability to digest gelatin may have:
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis results in thick, inspissated mucous plugs blocking pancreatic ducts, causing severe exocrine pancreatic enzyme insufficiency. The absence of pancreatic lipase and proteases leads to marked steatorrhea, creatorrhea (striated muscle fibers), and failure of fecal filtrate to digest gelatin or x-ray film emulsion (negative trypsin screen). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 344; PDF p. 369).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A stool specimen collected from an infant with diarrhea has a pH of 5.0. This result correlates with a:
questions.explanation: Unabsorbed dietary carbohydrates (such as lactose) pass into the colon, where commensal bacteria ferment them into lactic acid and short-chain organic acids, depressing fecal pH below 5.5. The presence of reducing disaccharides is demonstrated by a positive copper reduction test (Clinitest). (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 346; PDF p. 371).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following tests differentiates a malabsorption cause from a maldigestion cause in steatorrhea?
questions.explanation: D-xylose is a pentose sugar that is absorbed passively across the jejunal mucosa without requiring pancreatic digestive enzymes or bile salts. Impaired D-xylose excretion indicates an intestinal mucosal malabsorption defect (e.g., celiac disease), whereas normal D-xylose absorption with steatorrhea confirms maldigestion due to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 344; PDF p. 369).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following would not be a reason to collect a vaginal fluid for analysis?
choices: Complications of pregnancy resulting in preterm delivery
Forensic testing in a sexual assault
questions.explanation: Clinical indications for vaginal secretion analysis include differential diagnosis of vaginitis/vaginal discharge, obstetric assessment of preterm delivery risk (fetal fibronectin) or premature rupture of membranes (PAMG-1, IGFBP-1), and forensic sexual assault investigation. Confirmation of pregnancy is performed by assaying human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) in maternal urine or serum, not by vaginal fluid analysis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 352; PDF p. 377).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following organisms might not be detected if the specimen for vaginal secretion analysis had been refrigerated?
questions.explanation: Identification of the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis on wet mount microscopy relies on observing its characteristic rapid, jerky, nondirectional motility and undulating membrane. Exposure to ambient refrigeration temperatures (4°C) rapidly paralyzes and kills the trophozoites, causing them to round up and become indistinguishable from host leukocytes. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 353; PDF p. 378).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The appearance of the vaginal discharge in vulvovaginal candidiasis is described as:
questions.explanation: Symptomatic infection with Candida albicans (vulvovaginal candidiasis) characteristically manifests as an odorless, thick, white, curd-like or cottage-cheese-like vaginal exudate adhering to the vaginal mucosa, accompanied by marked pruritus, burning, and dyspareunia. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 353, Table 17-1; PDF p. 378).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A normal range for a vaginal pH is:
questions.explanation: In healthy women of reproductive age, commensal Lactobacillus species ferment glycogen into lactic acid, maintaining an acidic vaginal milieu between pH 3.8 and 4.5. This physiological acidity inhibits colonization by nonindigenous pathogens. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 353; PDF p. 378).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following tests differentiates budding yeast cells from RBCs?
questions.explanation: Adding a drop of 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) rapidly lyses squamous epithelial cells, leukocytes, and erythrocytes, clearing visual background debris while preserving the alkali-resistant chitinous cell walls of fungal blastoconidia (budding yeast) and pseudohyphae. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 354; PDF p. 379).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following constituents is normal in healthy vaginal fluid secretions?
questions.explanation: Predominant physiological inhabitants of the healthy vagina are large, non-sporeforming, gram-positive rods belonging to the genus Lactobacillus (accounting for > 90% of physiological flora). Presence of basal cells, parabasal cells, protozoa, or fungal pseudohyphae signifies epithelial pathology or infection. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 353; PDF p. 378).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Vaginal specimens collected for a saline wet prep should be:
questions.explanation: Vaginal swabs collected in sterile saline must be evaluated without delay (within 1 to 2 hours maximum) because trophozoite motility ceases rapidly upon cooling, and diagnostic clue cells disintegrate during prolonged standing. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 353; PDF p. 378).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A positive amine (whiff) test is observed in which of the following syndromes?
questions.explanation: The amine ('whiff') test involves adding 10% KOH to vaginal discharge; in bacterial vaginosis (BV), alkaline pH volatilizes foul-smelling polyamines (trimethylamine, putrescine, cadaverine) produced by overgrowing anaerobes, releasing a distinct pungent 'fishy' odor. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 354; PDF p. 379).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: A squamous epithelial cell covered with coccobacilli that extends beyond the cytoplasm margin is a:
questions.explanation: The microscopic pathognomonic hallmark of bacterial vaginosis is the clue cell: a mature vaginal squamous epithelial cell densely encrusted with thousands of adherent coccobacilli (Gardnerella vaginalis and Prevotella/Mobiluncus) that obscure the cell's cytoplasmic margins, giving it a distinctive stippled, peppered, or shaggy border. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 354; PDF p. 379).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are diagnostic of bacterial vaginosis except:
questions.explanation: Under Amsel's clinical criteria, bacterial vaginosis is diagnosed when at least three of the following four criteria are present: (1) thin homogeneous discharge, (2) presence of clue cells (> 20%), (3) positive amine/whiff test, and (4) vaginal pH > 4.5. A pH of 3.8 is normal and rules out BV. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 355; PDF p. 380).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following organisms produces lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide to maintain an acidic vaginal environment?
questions.explanation: Commensal Lactobacillus species (such as L. crispatus and L. jensenii) ferment estrogen-dependent intracellular glycogen into lactic acid (maintaining physiological pH 3.8–4.5) and generate hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and bacteriocins that suppress the proliferation of facultative and anaerobic opportunists. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 353; PDF p. 378).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are diagnostic of vulvovaginal candidiasis except:
questions.explanation: Diagnostic criteria for vulvovaginal candidiasis comprise finding pseudohyphae and budding yeast on 10% KOH or saline wet prep, numerous inflammatory WBCs, and a normal acidic pH (<= 4.5). Clue cells are characteristic of bacterial vaginosis and are not a feature of candidiasis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 355; PDF p. 380).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: All of the following are diagnostic of trichomoniasis except:
questions.explanation: Trichomoniasis is diagnosed by demonstration of motile trichomonads on wet mount, abundant leukocytes, elevated vaginal pH (5.0 to 6.0), and an occasionally positive amine test. A positive KOH test refers to visual detection of fungal pseudohyphae/blastospores, which is diagnostic of candidiasis, not trichomoniasis. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 355; PDF p. 380).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The bacteria associated with desquamative inflammatory vaginitis is:
questions.explanation: Desquamative inflammatory vaginitis (DIV) is characterized clinically by copious purulent vaginal exudate, deep mucosal erythema, elevated pH, a high ratio of parabasal to squamous cells, and a heavy overgrowth of beta-hemolytic streptococci (particularly Streptococcus agalactiae / Group B Streptococcus) displacing normal lactobacilli. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 356; PDF p. 381).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: The protein present in vaginal secretions that can identify patients who are at risk for preterm delivery is:
questions.explanation: Fetal fibronectin (fFN) is an adhesive basement membrane glycoprotein that anchors the fetal chorionic membranes to the maternal decidua. Its detection in cervicovaginal fluid between 24 and 34 weeks' gestation indicates mechanical or inflammatory disruption of the choriodecidual interface, serving as a powerful predictive biomarker for imminent preterm birth. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 356; PDF p. 381).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition

questions.prompt: Which of the following immunochromatographic tests detects both AFP and IGFBP-1 proteins to diagnose PROM?
questions.explanation: The ROM Plus assay is a dual-biomarker lateral flow immunoassay designed to diagnose premature rupture of fetal membranes (PROM). It combines monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies that simultaneously detect human alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and placental insulin-like growth factor-binding protein-1 (IGFBP-1), achieving superior sensitivity and specificity over single-analyte tests. (Strasinger, 7th ed., Ch. 17, Book p. 357; PDF p. 382).

source.kind: Strasinger's Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th Edition
